# Cloudflare API challenge: diagnose HTML instead of JSON

A JSON endpoint behind Cloudflare returns HTML? Read cf-mitigated, trace the Ray ID in Security Events, and scope a fix to the right product and clients.

By Centinel Analytica. Published 2026-11-09.

When a JSON endpoint behind Cloudflare suddenly returns HTML, a Cloudflare challenge page has almost certainly replaced your API response. Check for the cf-mitigated: challenge response header, find the responsible product with the Ray ID in Security Events, then scope the fix to that product and your intended authenticated clients.

This is a runbook for the person paged when a mobile app or partner integration starts throwing "Unexpected token < in JSON" or a bare 403. It assumes you own the zone or sit next to whoever does. You are not trying to turn protection off. You are trying to find which Cloudflare product intervened, why your client could not pass it, and how to make the narrowest possible exception without opening the endpoint to everyone.

## Short answer: a challenge page is HTML, and cf-mitigated proves it

A Cloudflare challenge page is an HTML document, and every challenge page response carries the cf-mitigated header set to challenge. Cloudflare documents this behavior for all challenge page types, and the content type is text/html no matter which resource the client asked for ([Cloudflare Docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-challenges/challenge-types/challenge-pages/detect-response/)).

That gives you a clean test. If a response from a JSON route has `cf-mitigated: challenge` and `Content-Type: text/html`, your origin never produced it. Cloudflare answered in front of the origin. Stop reading origin logs. They will show nothing for that request.

Two caveats keep you honest. First, not every 403 is a challenge. A WAF block, an IP access rule, a rate limit or your own origin can all return 403 without the header. Second, the header tells you a challenge happened, but not which product issued it. That comes from Security Events, covered below.

## Why challenges break API clients: fetch, XHR and machine-to-machine callers

A challenge interrupts the request flow by returning a full HTML page for the visitor's browser to render and solve ([Cloudflare Docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-challenges/challenge-types/challenge-pages/)). That model assumes a human looking at a screen. A fetch or XHR call has no screen. It receives the HTML as the response body, hands it to your JSON parser, and fails.

Machine-to-machine callers have it worse. A cron job, a partner's backend or a mobile SDK cannot run the JavaScript a Managed Challenge or Interactive Challenge needs, and it can't click a checkbox. Cloudflare's own page lists this as a compatibility limitation. It's why these clients fail every time instead of intermittently.

Browser-backed callers sit in the middle. A single-page app running in a real browser can sometimes pass a challenge on a page load, yet its later XHR calls to a different path still hit one. Same client, different outcome, depending on which rule matched which request.

So the first diagnostic question is about the client, not Cloudflare. Is this caller a browser session a human is driving, or software with no browser? The fix differs completely, which is why the later sections split on it.

## Detect it safely in the client: check the header and status before parsing JSON

Make every API client check the response before it calls its JSON parser. The order is: status, `cf-mitigated`, content type, then parse. A failed parse should never be the first signal anyone gets.

A minimal browser or Node pattern:

```
const res = await fetch(url, opts);
if (res.headers.get('cf-mitigated') === 'challenge') {
  throw new ChallengeError(res.status, res.headers.get('cf-ray'));
}
const type = res.headers.get('content-type') || '';
if (!type.includes('application/json')) {
  throw new UnexpectedContentError(res.status, type);
}
const data = await res.json();
```

Three details matter. Log the `cf-ray` response header with the error, since it is the key you will use in Security Events. Surface a typed error so callers can tell a challenge from a validation failure instead of showing "something went wrong". And do not retry automatically on a challenge. Retrying a challenged request just produces another challenge and, for writes, risks something worse (see the retry section).

A browser may expose only a subset of response headers to cross-origin scripts. If your API is on a different origin than the page, `cf-mitigated` may not be readable from JavaScript unless it is exposed. In that case, fall back to the content-type check, which is still reliable. This client-side guard turns a vague parse failure into a ticket that already contains the Ray ID.

## Find the responsible service: Security Events, Ray ID, time, path and method

Find the responsible Cloudflare product by locating the request's event in the dashboard under Security, Analytics, Events. Filter by the Ray ID from the failing response. If you have no Ray ID, narrow by time window, request path and HTTP method, then match the client's IP or user agent.

Each event shows a service and the rule or action that fired. That field is the point of the whole exercise. A challenge can come from a WAF custom rule, a rate limiting rule, Bot Fight Mode or Super Bot Fight Mode, and the correct fix is different for each. One request can also produce several events from different services, so read all of them rather than the first row.

A short worksheet for the incident:

- Ray ID from the client log.
- Timestamp in UTC, plus the path and method (a GET to `/v1/orders` may behave differently from a POST).
- Service and rule shown in the event.
- Action taken: managed challenge, interactive challenge, JS challenge, block.
- Client type: browser session or server-to-server.

If Security Events shows nothing for the Ray ID, the 403 probably did not come from a challenge at all. Check IP access rules, a block rule, rate limiting, and finally your origin. Don't assume Cloudflare because the symptom looks like Cloudflare.

For the pattern where a challenge completes and a second rule challenges again, see our write-up on [why CAPTCHA loops repeat](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/fix-bot-challenge-loops). The same habit of inspecting the next rule applies here.

## Fix by client type: browser sessions versus server-to-server integrations

Fix browser-backed API traffic and server-to-server traffic differently, because only one of them can solve a challenge.

**Browser sessions.** If a real browser calls your API after loading your site, Turnstile pre-clearance on the same zone is the documented route. After the visitor passes verification, the `cf_clearance` cookie lets later requests clear challenges at or below the configured clearance level ([Cloudflare Docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-challenges/challenge-types/challenge-pages/)). Validate the Turnstile token server-side, and keep the page that earns the cookie on the same zone as the API calls that need it.

**Server-to-server integrations.** Do not use pre-clearance here. A backend job with no browser cannot earn or present that cookie in any meaningful way, and bolting a headless browser onto an integration to chase a cookie is brittle. Remove the challenge for the authenticated client with a narrowly scoped rule (next section), and put real identity on the request.

Identity options, strongest first: mutual TLS through Cloudflare API Shield so only clients holding a certificate you issued reach the endpoint, signed requests that your origin verifies, or an API token your origin checks. An IP access rule allowlisting a partner's egress range is acceptable for a fixed, known partner, but it is a weaker control. Addresses change and shared infrastructure widens who is trusted.

Never trust a client-asserted header such as `X-Internal: true` as the basis for an exception. Anyone can send it. Key the exception on something the client can't forge, such as a verified certificate or a source you control.

## Scope the exception: Super Bot Fight Mode skip rules and the Bot Fight Mode limit

Which product issued the challenge decides whether an exception is even possible. Super Bot Fight Mode supports a WAF custom rule with the Skip action. Bot Fight Mode does not. Cloudflare states plainly that you cannot bypass or skip Bot Fight Mode using WAF custom rules or Page Rules ([Cloudflare Docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/bots/get-started/bot-fight-mode/)).

If Security Events names **Super Bot Fight Mode**, create a custom rule under Security rules, Custom rules:

1. Write a narrow expression: the exact host, the exact path prefix, the methods the integration uses, plus a client condition you trust (mTLS certificate validated, or the partner's fixed source range).
2. Choose Skip, and select all Super Bot Fight Mode rules.
3. Place it before any custom rule that could block or challenge the same request. Custom rules run before Super Bot Fight Mode, so order matters.

If it names **Bot Fight Mode**, you have a real constraint. Your options are to disable Bot Fight Mode for the zone if it is causing problems with application traffic, or to move the API to a hostname or zone where it is not enabled. Weigh that honestly. Turning it off affects every route, so compensate with explicit rules and rate limits on the routes it used to cover. The same bot features also show up as managed-rule and plan questions, which our [Cloudflare bot protection pricing checklist](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/cloudflare-bot-protection-pricing-enterprise-quote-checklist) and [Cloudflare Bot Management alternatives guide](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/cloudflare-bot-management-alternatives-architecture-first) walk through.

If the event names a WAF custom rule or rate limiting, fix that rule directly instead of reaching for a skip. Do not write a blanket `/api` bypass. A skip should cover the one route and the one authenticated client class, and leave authentication, authorization and unrelated security controls untouched.

On verified bots: allowing verified bots is a setting inside Super Bot Fight Mode, and it exists for crawlers such as search engines, not for your partner's backend. Don't stretch it to cover your own integrations.

## Stop retry damage: never blindly replay state-changing requests

Never let a client replay a POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE after it receives a challenge or an unparseable response. You do not know whether the origin saw the request. Usually it didn't, because Cloudflare answered first, but a timeout, a retry layer or a partial failure can leave you unsure, and a replayed payment or order is expensive.

Rules that hold up in production:

- Retry only idempotent methods automatically, and cap attempts with backoff.
- Treat a challenge as terminal for that call. Raise a typed error and stop. More attempts only generate more challenges and more Security Events noise.
- For state-changing calls, require an idempotency key the origin enforces, so a deliberate retry after a fix cannot double-apply.
- Make mobile SDKs and queue workers dead-letter challenged writes instead of looping.

Also watch for rate limits you create yourself. A retry storm against a challenged endpoint can trip a rate limiting rule and turn one problem into two. If you are budgeting request volume per account or endpoint, the thinking in our [API rate limiting guide](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/api-rate-limiting-for-bot-protection) applies. Make the rejection and the retry policy agree.

## Verify the fix, then check what the exception exposes

Verify with the real clients, not just curl from your laptop. Replay a known-good request from the integration's actual environment and confirm three things: the status is what the origin should return, `cf-mitigated` is absent, and the body parses as JSON. Then re-open Security Events for the new Ray ID and confirm the skip rule matched and nothing else fired.

Test the negative case too. Send the same request without the certificate, from an unlisted source, or with a forged trust header. It should still be challenged or blocked. An exception that passes both the intended client and an arbitrary one is a bypass, not a fix.

Then ask what the exception now exposes. Every skip removes a bot check for matching traffic, so that route depends on your authentication, authorization, input validation and rate limits to do the work. Watch the route for a week for volume anomalies, and write down who owns the rule and when it should be reviewed.

This is where an extra layer earns its place. Centinel Analytica is a bot and AI crawler protection service that tells real visitors from scrapers and applies allow, challenge or block policy through your existing CDN or edge, alongside Cloudflare, CloudFront, Akamai and Fastly, so your CDN or WAF stays in place.

## Diagnose the product first, then make the smallest exception

HTML on a JSON route is a routing fact, not a mystery. The cf-mitigated header proves Cloudflare answered, the Ray ID names the product, and the client type decides the fix. Scope every exception to one route and one authenticated client class. If you want an outside view of what automated traffic still reaches your API after those exceptions, reach out to Centinel Analytica.


## Frequently asked questions

### How do I fix a Cloudflare challenge blocking API requests?

Confirm it is a challenge by checking for cf-mitigated: challenge and a text/html body. Look up the Ray ID in Security Events to see which product fired. For Super Bot Fight Mode, add a narrow WAF custom Skip rule for the route and authenticated client. For browser sessions, use Turnstile pre-clearance. Never apply a blanket /api bypass.

### Can I skip Bot Fight Mode with a WAF custom rule?

No. Cloudflare states that Bot Fight Mode cannot be bypassed or skipped with WAF custom rules or Page Rules. Super Bot Fight Mode can be skipped with a Skip rule. If Bot Fight Mode is the cause, you can disable it or move the API to a hostname where it is off, then add explicit controls on the route.

### Does Turnstile pre-clearance work for server-to-server API clients?

No. Turnstile pre-clearance issues a cf_clearance cookie after successful verification, which can exempt subsequent requests—including API requests—from configured WAF challenges on the same zone, and it is not limited to browser-backed API calls. Backend integrations should use mTLS through API Shield, signed requests or tokens, plus a narrowly scoped skip rule, rather than trying to earn a challenge cookie.

### Is every Cloudflare 403 a challenge?

No. A 403 can come from a WAF block, an IP access rule, rate limiting or your own origin. A challenge response carries the cf-mitigated header and an HTML body. Check Security Events for the Ray ID; if no challenge event exists, investigate the other layers. Centinel Analytica works alongside Cloudflare if you want added bot policy.

# Cloudflare bot score: set thresholds by route

Set Cloudflare bot score thresholds per route: public pages, login, checkout, APIs and automation. Score ranges, rule patterns, rollout and rollback criteria.

By Centinel Analytica. Published 2026-11-09.

Set Cloudflare bot score thresholds per route, not one number for the whole zone: challenge low scores on login and checkout, log or rate-limit on public content, and never browser-challenge server-to-server API clients. Scores 2 to 29 are likely automated, score 1 is categorized as automated, 30 to 99 are likely human, and 0 means Bot Management did not evaluate the request, which can occur when requests are handled or redirected before scoring runs.

That is the short version. The rest of this post turns it into rule patterns you can adapt, separates what Cloudflare documents from what is an illustrative policy choice, and gives you rollout and rollback criteria so a threshold change does not lock out real customers. It complements our guides on [Cloudflare Bot Management alternatives](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/cloudflare-bot-management-alternatives-architecture-first) and [Cloudflare bot protection pricing](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/cloudflare-bot-protection-pricing-enterprise-quote-checklist). Here the question is narrower: which threshold goes on which route.

## Short answer: how to set Cloudflare bot score thresholds by route

Match the threshold to the cost of a wrong decision on that route. A false positive on checkout loses a sale. A false positive on a public article loses one page view. A false negative on login feeds credential stuffing. The same score deserves different actions in different places.

A workable starting policy, which is an illustrative choice and not a Cloudflare-validated threshold:

- **Public content:** log scores below 30, and rate-limit or challenge only after observation shows a clear scraper population.
- **Browser login (POST only):** managed challenge for scores below 30, excluding verified bots.
- **Checkout and payment steps:** managed challenge below 30, and review the 30 to 50 band before you consider widening.
- **APIs:** no browser challenge. Block or rate-limit by score only on routes your own clients never call, and skip known server-to-server clients.
- **Authenticated automation:** allow by explicit identity (token, mTLS, IP allowlist), not by score.

Cloudflare's own guidance is that [Bot Management assigns a score to every request, but you must create custom rules to block or challenge automated traffic](https://developers.cloudflare.com/bots/get-started/bot-management/). Scoring alone enforces nothing.

## What the score means: 0, 1, 2 to 29, 30 to 99 and verified bots

The score is a number from 1 to 99 that [indicates how likely a request came from a bot](https://developers.cloudflare.com/bots/concepts/bot-score/), and the field you write rules against is `cf.bot_management.score`. Read the bands as separate evidence, not one slider.

**0: not computed.** Bot Management did not evaluate the request. This is the most common mistake in score rules. A rule like `cf.bot_management.score lt 30` matches 0, so it can act on traffic that was never scored. Add a lower bound (`gt 0` or `ge 1`) so you act only on requests that were actually evaluated.

**1: automated.** Cloudflare's documented band for the highest-confidence automation. It is the safest place to block outright on sensitive routes, once you have confirmed your own tooling does not land there.

**2 to 29: likely automated.** Cloudflare describes 1 to 29 as likely automated. Managed challenges belong in this band. It is a probability, not a verdict, so legitimate headless monitoring and some privacy-heavy browsers can appear here.

**30 to 99: likely human.** Not proof of a human. A well-built browser-driven scraper can score here, which is why score alone does not stop scraping that runs real browsers.

**Verified bots** are a separate signal. The field, exposed as `cf.bot_management.verified_bot`, is a boolean indicating whether a request originates from a Cloudflare-allowed bot. Don't rely on their score. Exclude them explicitly with `not cf.bot_management.verified_bot` wherever a rule would otherwise challenge a crawler you want, such as a search engine.

Several engines generate the score: heuristics, machine learning, anomaly detection and JavaScript detections. Cloudflare notes these detection engines apply to Enterprise Bot Management, which is why granular score rules need that plan.

## Rule building blocks: score bounds, path, method, verified bots and static resources

Every route rule is the same five parts combined with `and`. Build them once, then reuse the pattern.

**Score bounds.** Always pair the upper and lower bound: `cf.bot_management.score gt 0 and cf.bot_management.score lt 30`. The `gt 0` keeps unscored requests out.

**Path.** Scope with `http.request.uri.path`, using `eq` for exact routes such as `/login` and `starts_with` for trees such as `/api/`.

**Method.** Cloudflare's own detection-ID example scopes a login rule to `http.request.method eq "POST"`. Do the same. Challenging a GET to the login page breaks the form before a user can submit it, and the POST is where credential stuffing happens.

**Verified bots.** Add `not cf.bot_management.verified_bot` so allowed crawlers are not challenged.

**Static resources.** Add `not cf.bot_management.static_resource` so images, scripts and stylesheets do not trigger challenges. A challenge on an asset request returns an interstitial where the browser expected an image, and it fails silently.

Here is an illustrative login rule that combines all five. It is an example to adapt, not an official template:

```
(http.request.uri.path eq "/login"
 and http.request.method eq "POST"
 and cf.bot_management.score gt 0
 and cf.bot_management.score lt 30
 and not cf.bot_management.verified_bot
 and not cf.bot_management.static_resource)
```

Action: Managed Challenge. Cloudflare publishes a comparable expression in its [detection IDs documentation](https://developers.cloudflare.com/bots/additional-configurations/detection-ids/), pairing `cf.bot_management.score lt 30` with `not cf.bot_management.verified_bot` and a `/login` POST scope. Cloudflare also ships custom rule templates during setup. Start from those and tighten them instead of writing from scratch.

## Thresholds by route: public content, browser login, checkout, APIs and authenticated automation

The values below are illustrative policy choices. Cloudflare documents the bands, not a recommended per-route cutoff, so validate each one against your own traffic before enforcing.

| Route | Illustrative starting rule | Action | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Public content (articles, product pages) | Score 1 to 29, not verified bot, not static | Log first, then rate-limit | Real readers on odd browsers land in the low band; a hard block costs traffic and ad revenue |
| Browser login (POST) | Score 1 to 29, not verified bot | Managed Challenge | Credential stuffing concentrates here; a human can pass a challenge |
| Checkout and payment | Score 1 to 29, not verified bot | Managed Challenge, review 30 to 50 band | Highest cost of a false positive and of fraud |
| Public API called by browsers | Score 1 to 29 on routes your site JavaScript calls | Managed Challenge only if the client is a browser | Browsers can solve it |
| API called by servers or apps | Do not browser-challenge | Rate-limit, token auth, or block score 1 | A server-to-server client cannot solve an interactive challenge |
| Authenticated automation (partners, monitors) | Identify by token, mTLS or IP | Skip score rules | Your own tooling often scores low by design |

**Public content.** Start in log mode. Publishers in particular get unknown crawlers and AI agents arriving with ordinary-looking traffic, and our piece on [bot mitigation for publishers](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/bot-mitigation-for-publishers-manage-unknown-crawlers-at-edge) covers how to manage that at the edge. Challenging every sub-30 article request is the fastest way to hurt reader experience.

**Browser login.** Challenge POSTs, not page loads, and keep verified bots out of the rule. If users report challenge loops, see our guide on [reCAPTCHA vs Cloudflare Turnstile](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/recaptcha-vs-cloudflare-turnstile-server-side-checks) for how challenge widgets behave.

**Checkout.** Be most conservative here. A checkout rule that challenges a returning customer mid-payment is a lost order. Observe the 30 to 50 band for fraud patterns before widening, and remember that [inventory hoarding bots](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/ecommerce-bot-protection-prevent-inventory-hoarding) often hit cart and add-to-basket endpoints, not only payment.

**APIs.** Don't browser-challenge server-to-server clients. A mobile app, a partner integration or a cron job cannot render an interstitial, so a challenge simply fails the request. Check current Cloudflare challenge and API guidance before deploying, since supported challenge behavior for non-browser clients can change. For these routes, prefer rate limits, API tokens and a block only on score 1.

**Authenticated automation.** Your own uptime checks, partner feeds and QA suites will often score low. Identify them by credential or network identity and skip them, so you never depend on their score staying high.

## Roll out in observation first: completion checks and rollback criteria

Ship every new rule in log-only mode first, then promote it. Cloudflare's Security Analytics lets you filter and analyze traffic and create rules based on applied filters.

A rollout sequence that holds up:

1. **Log.** Run the expression with a log action for at least one full traffic cycle, including your weekly peak.
2. **Sample the matches.** Pull requests that matched and check the paths, user agents and countries. Confirm your monitors, partners and mobile apps are not in the set.
3. **Challenge a slice.** Move to Managed Challenge on one route.
4. **Measure completion.** Compare conversion on that route before and after: login success rate, checkout completion rate, API error rate. A drop beyond normal variance is your signal.
5. **Promote or roll back.** Widen the rule only if completion holds.

Set rollback criteria in writing before you start:

- Completion rate on the protected route falls below your agreed floor for a sustained window.
- Support tickets about blocked or looping users rise above baseline.
- A known legitimate client (partner, monitor, mobile app) appears in challenged traffic.
- Verified-bot crawl volume drops, which suggests the verified-bot exclusion is missing.

Any single trigger means revert to log mode, fix the expression, and restart from step 1. A threshold is a hypothesis you test, not a setting you trust.

## Where a second opinion helps: adding Centinel evidence beside Cloudflare

Cloudflare's score is one view of a request. Centinel Analytica is bot and AI crawler protection that tells real visitors from scrapers and applies allow, challenge or block policy through your existing CDN or edge.

That matters for threshold-setting because the hardest cases sit in the 30 to 99 band, where scrapers that look like real browsers score as likely human and pass untouched. Centinel's published research shows how far declared identity can drift from reality: 84% of requests claiming to be GPTBot are fake on a typical news site. A second evidence source helps you decide whether a route's borderline traffic is really human before you widen a challenge.



## Treat each Cloudflare bot score threshold as a per-route hypothesis

There is no correct single Cloudflare bot score cutoff, only a correct cutoff for each route and each cost of being wrong. Bound every rule with `gt 0`, scope it by path and method, exclude verified bots and static resources, keep servers out of browser challenges, and promote only after completion rates hold. If your borderline 30 to 99 traffic still worries you, evaluate what additional evidence Centinel Analytica surfaces beside your existing Cloudflare setup.


## Frequently asked questions

### Do I need Enterprise to use Cloudflare bot score rules?

Granular score-based rules on cf.bot_management.score require Enterprise Bot Management, a paid add-on. Cloudflare says the detection engines behind the score apply to Enterprise Bot Management. Lower plans use simpler bot features. If you cannot or do not want to move to Enterprise, Centinel Analytica can apply allow, challenge or block policy through your existing CDN.

### What does a Cloudflare bot score of 0 mean?

A score of 0 means the bot score was not computed, not necessarily that Bot Management did not evaluate the request. It is not a low score and not a sign of a bot. Because 0 is numerically below 30, a rule using only `score lt 30` will match it. Add a lower bound such as `cf.bot_management.score gt 0` so you act only on requests that were actually scored.

### Why do I get challenge loops after adding a score rule?

Loops usually come from challenging the wrong request: a GET instead of the login POST, a static asset, an API call from a non-browser client, or a verified bot you forgot to exclude. Scope the rule by path and method, add the verified-bot and static-resource exclusions, and test in log mode first.

### How is Super Bot Fight Mode different from Bot Management score rules?

Super Bot Fight Mode applies broad, preset actions to categories of bot traffic. Bot Management with the score gives you a per-request number you can write custom rules against, route by route, using fields like cf.bot_management.score. Use the score when different routes need different responses. Centinel Analytica works beside either, without replacing your CDN or WAF.

# Cloudways Bot Protection Whitelist: Narrow IP Exceptions

Use the Cloudways Bot Protection whitelist as a last-step exception: prove which layer returned the 403, allow one trusted IP, test it, then remove it.

By Centinel Analytica. Published 2026-11-06.

Whitelist one trusted IP in Cloudways Bot Protection, and only after you've confirmed that Bot Protection, not Cloudflare or the origin server, returned the 403. Treat it as a narrow, temporary exception: add the address, test it, and remove it when the job is done.

That discipline matters because Cloudways documentation describes IP whitelisting for Bot Protection, separately covering specific IPs and bots. An exception for a monitoring service is also an exception for anyone who can send traffic from that address. Add the wrong range and you've switched off protection for every client behind it.

This guide walks through the order of operations: identify the blocking layer, add one IP as documented, verify the result, set a removal date, and recognize when an IP allowlist is the wrong tool entirely.

## Short answer: whitelist one trusted IP, only after you confirm Bot Protection blocked it

Do these four things, in this order:

1. Reproduce the 403 from the exact IP that is being blocked and capture the response body and headers.
2. Decide which layer produced it: Bot Protection, Cloudflare, or the origin.
3. If it was Bot Protection, add that single IP to the application's whitelist.
4. Test, then schedule the entry's removal.

Skipping step 2 is the common mistake. A 403 is a status code, not a diagnosis. If you whitelist an IP in Bot Protection and the real cause was a file permission or a Cloudflare rule, nothing changes and you've still left a hole in your bot defenses.

The exception is also the last step, not the first. If a legitimate monitor, webhook sender, partner or crawler is blocked, ask whether you can fix the client first (a correct user agent, a lower request rate, a stable egress IP). The whitelist is for the case where the client is genuinely trusted and genuinely can't change.

## Which layer returned your 403? Bot Protection, Cloudflare or the origin

Three different layers can return a 403 on a Cloudways-hosted application, and each has a different fix. Cloudways' own [403 Forbidden troubleshooting article](https://support.cloudways.com/en/articles/5124473-how-to-fix-403-forbidden) covers the origin-side causes. Start there if the block doesn't look bot-related.

Use the response itself to separate them:

| Layer | What to look for | Where the fix lives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cloudways Bot Protection | Block happens at the application edge of the Cloudways stack; the client is an automated source such as a monitor, script or crawler; the request succeeds from a browser on a different IP | Application > Security > Bot Protection whitelist |
| Cloudflare (if you use it in front) | Response carries Cloudflare headers such as `server: cloudflare` and a `cf-ray` value, or shows a Cloudflare error page | Cloudflare dashboard rules, not Cloudways |
| Origin or server permissions | Generic web-server 403 page; same result from every IP; often tied to file or directory permissions, ownership, or an application rule | File permissions, `.htaccess`, application or plugin config |

Three quick tests narrow it down:

- **Same URL from a second IP.** If it loads from your laptop but fails from the monitor's IP, the block is IP- or behavior-specific, which points at Bot Protection or a firewall. If it fails from everywhere, suspect the origin.
- **Inspect headers.** Run `curl -sI https://your-site.example/path` from the blocked machine. Cloudflare headers tell you the request never reached Cloudways.
- **Temporarily disable Bot Protection on a staging copy or at a quiet time.** If the 403 disappears, Bot Protection was the layer. Re-enable it immediately. Don't leave it off.

Only when the evidence points at Bot Protection do you move to the whitelist.

## How to add a Cloudways Bot Protection IP exception (as documented)

Cloudways documents the process in two articles: [how to protect your applications with Bot Protection](https://support.cloudways.com/en/articles/5124791-how-to-protect-your-applications-with-bot-protection) and [how to whitelist IPs to bypass Bot Protection](https://support.cloudways.com/en/articles/5132911-how-to-whitelist-ips-to-bypass-bot-protection). The documented flow is:

1. Select the application you want to configure.
2. Make sure Bot Protection is enabled for that application.
3. Open the Security tab.
4. Choose Whitelist IP.
5. Enter the IP address and save.

Two points deserve emphasis.

**The exception is per application.** You select an application first, so the allowance applies to that app's Bot Protection, not to your whole server. If a partner only needs to reach one webhook endpoint on one app, add the IP there and nowhere else.

**Check the current UI and your plan before you rely on this.** Menu labels and plan availability change. Confirm against the two articles above at the time you make the change, and enter the address in the format the form accepts. Don't assume range or CIDR notation is supported unless the current documentation says so. When in doubt, add individual addresses.

## Why narrow beats broad: shared proxies, CDN ranges and spoofed identity

Cloudways documents whitelisting for specific IPs and bots under Bot Protection. Read that literally: once an address is on the list, requests from it skip the checks. The size of the exception is the size of the audience that can send traffic from that address.

That's why broad entries are dangerous:

- **Shared proxy and VPN egress addresses.** One corporate proxy or consumer VPN exit can carry thousands of unrelated users. Whitelist it and you've exempted all of them, including any scraper using the same service.
- **CDN and cloud ranges.** Allowing a CDN's addresses exempts every customer of that CDN who can make an outbound request through it. An attacker can rent capacity in the same range.
- **Cloud function and hosting IPs.** Serverless platforms hand out addresses that rotate between tenants. Today's trusted webhook sender may be tomorrow's scraper on the same address.
- **Identity claimed in a header.** A user agent that says it's a trusted crawler proves nothing on its own. IP is a stronger signal than a header, but only when the IP is genuinely controlled by the party you trust.

The safe pattern is one address that belongs to a party you can name, with a stated reason and an owner. If you can't say who controls the address, don't allow it.

If the address sits behind a load balancer or reverse proxy, also confirm which IP your stack actually sees. Our [Nginx bot protection guide](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/nginx-bot-protection-rate-limits-real-ips-and-safe-rollout) explains trusted proxy headers and real-IP handling. The same logic applies when you decide which address to enter.

## Test the exception, then set a review and removal date

After saving, prove the change did what you intended and nothing more.

**Test the positive case.** From the whitelisted IP, repeat the exact request that failed. Confirm you now get the expected status and content, not just a different error.

**Test the negative case.** From an IP that isn't whitelisted, repeat a request that Bot Protection should still challenge. If it now passes, something broader than you intended was allowed.

**Record the entry.** Write down the IP, the application, who requested it, why, and the date. A whitelist entry with no owner becomes permanent by neglect.

**Set a removal date.** Pick a short window: a week for a migration test, a quarter for a standing monitor. Put the review in a calendar or ticket, not in someone's memory. At review, ask whether the client still needs the exception, whether its IP is still stable, and whether a better fix now exists. Then remove the entry through the same Security tab and re-run the negative test.

A temporary exception that lasts three years is a permanent hole you forgot about.

## Controls that are not this one: server firewall, SFTP/SSH, Cloudflare WAF and WordPress plugins

Several controls sound similar and live in different places. Editing the wrong one wastes time and can weaken the wrong layer.

- **Server firewall and SFTP/SSH allowlists.** Cloudways manages access to the server itself (SSH, SFTP) separately. Allowing an IP there doesn't change how Bot Protection treats web requests, and a Bot Protection whitelist doesn't grant shell or file access.
- **Cloudflare WAF and rules.** If Cloudflare sits in front of your site, its firewall, rate limiting and bot settings act before traffic reaches Cloudways. A block from Cloudflare must be fixed in Cloudflare.
- **WordPress security plugins.** Plugins enforce their own IP rules, rate limits and login protection inside the application. A plugin 403 won't be cleared from the Cloudways panel. For login, XML-RPC and REST hardening, see our [WordPress bot protection guide](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/wordpress-bot-protection-login-and-xml-rpc-controls) rather than loosening Bot Protection to compensate.

The diagnostic table earlier exists for this reason. Identify the layer first, then change only that layer.

## When an IP allowlist is not enough: crawlers that spoof identity and bots on an existing CDN

An IP exception answers one question: is this specific address trusted? It can't answer harder ones. What about a crawler that claims a well-known identity but comes from somewhere else? What about scrapers that rotate through residential addresses, so no single IP is worth allowing or blocking?

In those cases an allowlist either blocks real clients or lets impostors through. Published research shows how wide the gap can be: on a typical news site, 84% of requests claiming to be GPTBot were fake, according to Centinel Analytica's own fake-crawler research. A rule that trusts the name rather than verifying the source would have admitted most of that traffic.

Centinel Analytica is bot and AI crawler protection that tells real visitors from scrapers that look like them, then applies allow, challenge or block policy through your existing CDN or edge. If your problem has moved from one blocked partner to scrapers that imitate real traffic, that's the layer to evaluate. The [bot false positive testing guide](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/bot-false-positive-testing-verify-visitors-before-blocking) is a useful companion for checking that legitimate visitors still get through before you tighten any policy.

## Keep the exception small, and audit what the allowlist cannot see

A Bot Protection whitelist entry is a deliberate hole, so make it the smallest one that solves a proven problem: one trusted IP, on one application, tested, owned and scheduled for removal. If you find yourself maintaining a growing list of exceptions because scrapers keep imitating legitimate traffic, the allowlist isn't the fix.


## Frequently asked questions

### Does the Cloudways Bot Protection whitelist bypass all security checks?

Cloudways documents that whitelisted IPs bypass Bot Protection rules for the application you configure. It does not replace your server firewall, SFTP/SSH access controls, Cloudflare settings or WordPress plugin rules, which are separate layers. Keep entries to single trusted addresses and remove them when no longer needed.

### How do I know if Cloudways Bot Protection caused my 403?

Test the same URL from a second IP and inspect headers with curl. If it loads elsewhere but fails from the blocked IP, and there are no Cloudflare headers, Bot Protection is a likely cause. A 403 from every IP points to origin permissions, and Cloudflare headers point to Cloudflare.

### Should I whitelist a CDN or proxy IP range in Cloudways?

Avoid it. Because whitelisted IPs bypass bot-protection rules, a shared proxy or CDN range exempts every user and tenant behind those addresses, including scrapers. Do not assume range syntax is supported unless current Cloudways documentation says so. Add one address you can attribute to a named, trusted party.

### How long should a Bot Protection IP exception stay in place?

Set a removal date when you add it: days for a one-off test, a quarter for a standing monitor. Record who requested it and why, then review on schedule. After removing it, confirm the client is challenged again. Unowned entries tend to become permanent, which quietly weakens protection.

### What if scrapers spoof a trusted crawler identity instead of coming from one IP?

An IP allowlist cannot verify identity that attackers imitate. Centinel Analytica tells real visitors from scrapers and applies allow, challenge or block policy through your existing CDN or edge. Its research found 84% of requests claiming to be GPTBot on a typical news site were fake.

# Wordfence bot protection: crawler limits and Googlebot

How Wordfence crawler and human page-view limits, 404 thresholds and throttle versus block work, why only verified Google crawlers get exempted, and where PHP limits end.

By Centinel Analytica. Published 2026-11-06.

Wordfence bot protection counts requests per visitor at the PHP layer and throttles or blocks whoever crosses your thresholds. Set the crawler and human page-view limits, the 404 limit and the action from your own logs, and exempt only verified Google crawlers, never any client that merely says it is Googlebot.

That is also where the plugin stops. Requests answered from a CDN cache never reach WordPress, so they are never counted. This guide covers each setting, how to choose values for your site, and how to decide whether PHP-layer limits are enough or whether enforcement needs to sit upstream. Every number below is a placeholder to test, not a safe default.

## Short answer: what Wordfence rate limiting can and cannot do for crawlers

Wordfence rate limiting can slow or stop crawlers that hit your WordPress origin too fast. It cannot see traffic that never reaches WordPress. It runs inside the plugin's firewall, so it evaluates only the requests PHP actually handles. The [Wordfence rate limiting help page](https://www.wordfence.com/help/firewall/rate-limiting/) is the reference for what each setting does. Read the current version before changing anything, because option names and defaults change between releases.

Three jobs fit well. It can cap runaway crawlers that walk your archive pages at high speed. It can catch scanners that probe for files that do not exist and generate floods of 404s. And it can keep a misbehaving but non-malicious bot from exhausting PHP workers.

Three jobs fit badly. It cannot tell a real crawler from a copy of its user agent without a verification step. It cannot see cache hits served by a CDN or page cache in front of PHP. And it is not a scraping defense: a patient scraper that stays under your thresholds and rotates addresses will pass.

Treat the plugin as one layer. For login and XML-RPC specifically, see the [WordPress bot protection guide](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/wordpress-bot-protection-login-and-xml-rpc-controls). This post stays on page views, 404s and crawler handling.

## Crawler versus human page-view limits and 404 thresholds

Wordfence splits traffic into two buckets, and you should set the two limits differently. One limit applies to anything the firewall identifies as a crawler, the other to visitors it treats as human. Humans click, read, and click again, so their limit can be loose. Crawlers fetch pages in tight bursts, so their limit is where a mistake costs you search visibility.

Start with the human page-view limit, because it is the safer one to get right. A reader rarely requests dozens of pages a minute. But a reader on a slow connection with several tabs, or a visitor behind a shared office or mobile carrier address, can look busy. Set the limit above the busiest legitimate pattern in your logs, not above your average.

The crawler limit needs more care. Search engines and monitoring services are crawlers too, and a limit tight enough to stop an abusive bot can also slow Google. That is why the next two sections cover action choice and verification before you tighten anything.

The 404 threshold is the most useful of the three for catching probing. A visitor who requests many missing URLs in a short window is usually scanning for old plugin paths, backup files or admin panels. Real users hit the occasional dead link. Before you set it, check how many 404s your own site legitimately serves. A site that recently migrated or changed its URL structure will have crawlers and old inbound links producing bursts of 404s that look hostile and are not.

One rule applies to all three. Pick a starting value from your log data, apply it with the most lenient action, and watch what it catches. If you cannot name the traffic a limit would have stopped, you don't yet have a reason for that number.

## Throttle or block: choosing the action and block duration

Throttle first, block second, and keep block durations short until the log shows you are catching the right traffic. Throttling slows a client that crossed the line. Blocking denies it for a set period. The two fail differently.

A throttled legitimate crawler recovers on its own. It gets slowed, backs off, and returns to normal. A blocked legitimate crawler may mark your site unreachable, and recovery takes as long as the crawler's own retry schedule, which you don't control. For anything that might be a search engine, that asymmetry is the whole argument for throttling.

Blocking earns its place for traffic you have already judged hostile, such as a client producing hundreds of 404s against paths no legitimate visitor requests. Even then, start with a short duration. A long block applied to a shared address, like a university network or mobile carrier gateway, also locks out innocent users behind it. Lengthen the duration only after you have seen repeat offenders return from the same sources.

A practical order of operations:

1. Set the 404 threshold with a throttle action and review what it catches for a week.
2. Promote to a short block only for patterns that are clearly scanning, such as repeated requests for nonexistent file types.
3. Keep the crawler page-view limit on throttle until verification is working, covered next.
4. Revisit durations after you have seen how often blocked addresses return.

Write down what each setting was before you changed it. Rollback is the cheapest safety feature you have.

## Verified Google crawlers versus anyone claiming Googlebot

Exempt Google only when the request is verified as Google, never because the user agent string says Googlebot. A user agent is a self-reported label. Any script can send it, and scrapers do, precisely because sites tend to wave Googlebot through.

That is the trap in any allowlist keyed on a name. If your rate limit says "skip Googlebot" and the check is a string match, you have built a free pass for every scraper willing to type that string. Wordfence's rate limiting settings include an option that separates real Google crawlers from clients that only claim to be Google. Check the current wording on the [rate limiting help page](https://www.wordfence.com/help/firewall/rate-limiting/) and use the verified option rather than a user agent exemption.

Google documents how to verify its own crawlers independently: a reverse DNS lookup on the requesting address, a forward lookup on the resulting hostname, and confirmation that it resolves back to the same address. Google also publishes IP range lists for its crawlers. Use these to spot-check addresses in your logs, so you can see whether the traffic labelled Googlebot in your access log matches what the plugin treats as verified.

Keep the scope narrow. Verification methods are specific to each operator. What works for Google does not transfer to OpenAI, Anthropic, Perplexity or any other crawler, each of which publishes its own method, and some publish none a site can check. Don't apply "verified Google" logic to other bots, and don't assume an AI crawler named in a user agent is the real one. For one worked example of checking a named AI crawler, see [What is ClaudeBot?](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/what-is-claudebot-anthropics-crawler-explained).

For your settings, that means exempting verified Google crawlers from the aggressive limits if you want to protect search crawling, and leaving every unverified client subject to them, including the ones wearing Google's name.

## Where PHP-layer limits stop: CDN cache hits, Live Traffic and upstream enforcement

Wordfence counts what reaches PHP, so a request answered by a CDN or a full-page cache never enters its count. Put a CDN in front of WordPress with caching on, and a crawler hammering cached pages may look quiet to Wordfence while it still eats bandwidth and copies your content. Whether a given request reaches the plugin depends on your cache configuration, so verify it for your own stack rather than assuming.

The test is simple. Request a cacheable page from a client you control, then look for it in the plugin's records. If a page you fetched does not appear, it was served before PHP ran, and no Wordfence limit applies to it.

[Live Traffic](https://www.wordfence.com/help/tools/live-traffic/) is the plugin's view of visitors and crawlers hitting the site, and it has the same boundary. It shows what the plugin observed, not everything your CDN served. Use it to see which clients are tripping limits and what they request, and read its output as a record of origin traffic, not a full picture of crawler load.

The address problem sits on the same boundary. Behind a proxy or CDN, the connecting address Wordfence sees can be the proxy's, not the visitor's, unless the plugin is configured to read the forwarded client address correctly. If that is wrong, rate limits can lump many visitors together or exempt the wrong ones. Check the setting that tells Wordfence how to obtain the visitor's IP before trusting any per-client limit. The same real-address reasoning, applied at the web server, is covered in the [Nginx bot protection guide](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/nginx-bot-protection-rate-limits-real-ips-and-safe-rollout).

That boundary is why PHP-layer limiting and edge enforcement are different jobs, not rival ones. The plugin protects the application that runs behind the cache. Anything that must be decided before the cache answers has to be decided upstream.

## Inspect logs and test legitimate workflows before tightening

Look at a week or two of real traffic before you change a threshold, and test your own workflows after. Without that baseline, every number is a guess.

Start with the evidence you already have. From server access logs and Live Traffic, pull the busiest clients by request count, the clients with the most 404s, and the user agents claiming to be search crawlers. For each cluster, ask whether you can explain it. Your monitoring service, your own feed reader, a partner's integration and a search engine are all expected. A cluster you can't explain is the one to investigate before limiting.

Then list the legitimate workflows that generate bursts:

- Search engine crawling after a sitemap update or large content publish
- Uptime and performance monitors that poll on a schedule
- Editors previewing and saving many pages in one session
- Payment, shipping or newsletter services calling back into the site
- Your own staging or QA scripts

For each, work out whether the limit you are about to set would catch it. A monitor that checks every ten seconds is not abuse, and neither is a publishing day where an editor opens forty drafts.

After a change, retest. Browse as a normal reader. Run your monitor. Use Google's own tools to confirm a page can still be fetched. If blocked requests rise and you can't attribute them to hostile traffic, the limit is too tight. For a fuller method, [bot false positive testing](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/bot-false-positive-testing-verify-visitors-before-blocking) walks through verifying visitors before blocking them.

## Keeping Wordfence resource use bounded

A security plugin that slows the site it protects has failed, so budget its overhead as deliberately as its rules. Wordfence documents the settings that affect its own consumption on its [resource tuning page](https://www.wordfence.com/help/advanced/tuning-wordfence-resource-usage/), and that page is the source to follow for current option names and recommendations.

Match the plugin's work to your hosting. Scans, logging and live monitoring all cost CPU, memory and database writes. On modest shared hosting, the heavy options can compete with page generation. Review what you have enabled, lengthen or reduce anything you don't act on, and don't turn on every logging option by default.

Logging deserves its own caution. Recording every request is useful during an investigation and expensive in steady state, because it grows the database and adds writes to each page load. Turn up detail when you are diagnosing a crawler problem, then turn it back down.

Also keep rate limiting from becoming the load. A flood of requests that the plugin has to evaluate one by one still uses PHP workers, even if each is denied quickly. If a crawler produces enough volume that denying it costs real capacity, move enforcement upstream rather than tuning PHP harder.

## When to add edge enforcement beside your CDN

Add enforcement at the edge when the traffic you care about is decided before WordPress runs, or when volume itself is the problem. Three signs point that way: scraping that stays under your PHP thresholds, crawlers hitting cached pages the plugin never sees, and bots that claim a trusted identity you can't verify from inside the plugin.

Centinel Analytica is bot and AI crawler protection that tells real visitors from scrapers that look like them, then applies allow, challenge or block policy through your existing CDN or edge. It does not replace Wordfence or integrate with it. The plugin keeps handling what reaches WordPress, and edge policy handles what should be decided earlier.

For crawlers, identity is the problem. Published Centinel research found that on a typical news site, 84% of requests claiming to be GPTBot were fake. A name in a user agent is not proof. That is the same lesson as Googlebot above, applied to every crawler that matters to your content.

If you already run a CDN, the placement question is where checks sit relative to the cache. The [Fastly bot protection guide](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/fastly-bot-protection-pre-cache-and-post-cache-checks) covers pre-cache and post-cache decisions in detail, and the same reasoning applies to other CDNs.

## Conclusion

Wordfence is a sound origin-side control when you set it from your own logs: loose human limits, careful crawler limits, a 404 threshold that catches probing, throttle before block, and exemptions only for verified Google crawlers. Its edge is the PHP boundary, and anything served from cache or decided before WordPress runs needs enforcement elsewhere.


## Frequently asked questions

### Does Wordfence block Googlebot by default?

Wordfence can slow or block any client that crosses your configured limits, including a real search crawler if the limits are too tight. Use the option that exempts verified Google crawlers, and keep crawler limits on throttle until you have checked your logs. Do not exempt by user agent string alone, because scrapers copy it.

### How do I tell real Googlebot from a fake?

Do a reverse DNS lookup on the requesting IP, then a forward lookup on the hostname and confirm it returns the same address. Google also publishes crawler IP ranges you can compare against. A user agent saying Googlebot proves nothing on its own. Edge tools such as Centinel Analytica can apply the same distinction before traffic reaches WordPress.

### Why doesn't Wordfence rate limiting see traffic served by my CDN?

Wordfence is PHP-based, but Extended Protection can run before WordPress loads and process PHP requests; Basic WordPress Protection runs after WordPress loads and may miss direct requests to files that bypass WordPress. Pages answered from a CDN or full-page cache never get that far. Test it by fetching a cacheable page and checking whether it appears in the plugin's records. For decisions before the cache, you need enforcement at the edge.

### What rate limit values should I use in Wordfence?

There is no universal safe value. Pull a week or two of access logs and Live Traffic, find your busiest legitimate clients, and set limits above that pattern. Start with throttling, review what each limit catches, and only then consider short blocks. Retest search crawling and your own workflows after each change.

### Is Wordfence enough to stop AI scrapers?

Not by itself. It limits request rates at the PHP layer, but a scraper that stays under your thresholds or hits cached pages will pass, and AI crawler names in user agents are easy to fake. Centinel Analytica adds bot and AI crawler protection through your existing CDN or edge, alongside Wordfence.

By Centinel Analytica. Published 2026-11-06.

Everything below comes from three Barracuda documentation pages, checked on November 4, 2026. Where a page does not say something, this article says "confirm with Barracuda" instead of filling the gap. It contains no prices and no rankings. Licensing terms, plan contents and commercial details come from Barracuda, not from a third-party blog.

The audience is the person who has to scope this: a head of security, a platform or DevOps engineer, or a CTO at a publisher or ecommerce company. Maybe you want to know what Advanced Bot Protection (ABP) is before you buy. Maybe you already run Barracuda WAF and need to know what is licensed, where it runs and how to test it without hurting real customers. The last third of the article is an evaluation plan you can run in a few weeks.

## Short answer: what Barracuda Advanced Bot Protection is and what is licensed

According to Barracuda's documentation, Advanced Bot Protection is a bot mitigation capability of Barracuda WAF. The appliance documentation describes on-box and cloud components, and says the feature is licensed. Barracuda WAF-as-a-Service documents hosted bot controls separately. ([Barracuda Campus](https://documentation.campus.barracuda.com/wiki/spaces/BWAFv76/pages/2721132/Advanced%2BBot%2BProtection))

Two consequences follow. First, "we have Barracuda" does not tell you whether you have ABP. The appliance page ties the feature to licensing, so ask what your entitlement actually covers. Second, a feature on one deployment page is not a promise on the other. Treat each documentation page as proof for its own product only.

That rule runs through the rest of this article. A capability documented for the appliance is listed under the appliance. A capability documented for the hosted service is listed there. When a page is silent, the question goes in the list at the end.

## Appliance WAF versus WAF-as-a-Service: documented differences, with unknowns marked

The appliance Barracuda WAF and Barracuda WAF-as-a-Service are separate documentation spaces. The appliance docs live under the WAF v7.6 space. The hosted service has its own space with its own Bot Protection page. Reading one does not substitute for the other.

Here is what the pages document, and nothing more:

| Topic | Appliance WAF | WAF-as-a-Service |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where bot logic runs | On-box and cloud components | Hosted by Barracuda |
| How you reach it | Bot Mitigation tab on the appliance | Bot Protection controls in the hosted console |
| Visibility | ABP dashboard, humans versus bots | Not confirmed in the pages read: confirm with Barracuda |
| Licensing | Feature licensing documented | Plan versus license mapping: confirm with Barracuda |

The last row matters most. Do not assume that a control listed under the hosted service exists on the appliance, or the reverse. If a vendor call includes the sentence "it works the same on both," ask for the documentation page that says so.

Also confirm how bot telemetry from each deployment is retained and exported, and whether your SIEM can ingest it. The pages read for this article do not settle that, so it stays an open question.

## Appliance WAF: on-box and cloud components, the Bot Mitigation tab and the ABP dashboard

The appliance documentation describes ABP as having an on-box part and a cloud part, and states that the feature is licensed. ([Barracuda Campus](https://documentation.campus.barracuda.com/wiki/spaces/BWAFv76/pages/2721132/Advanced%2BBot%2BProtection)) In practice, enabling bot mitigation on an appliance is not only a local configuration change. A cloud component is part of the design, so check egress and connectivity requirements with your network team before a rollout date is set.

On the appliance, bot settings sit under the Bot Mitigation tab, and the feature sits behind licensing. Before you plan a test, verify in the appliance's own administrative interface that the feature is available to you. If it is not visible, that is a licensing question for Barracuda, not a configuration bug to chase.

The second documentation page covers the ABP dashboard. It provides visibility into overall traffic patterns and automated activity. That changes how you test. If classification builds across several requests, a single request from a test script may not produce a verdict, so a one-shot curl test tells you little. Plan scripted sessions that look like real browsing, and give the dashboard time before you judge it.

Read the dashboard as a measurement tool first and an enforcement tool second. It shows you the split between humans and bots on your own traffic. You need that baseline before you block anything.

## WAF-as-a-Service: hosted controls, honeypots, client challenges, bots and AI crawlers

The hosted service has its own Bot Protection page, and it describes the controls as hosted. ([Barracuda Campus](https://documentation.campus.barracuda.com/wiki/spaces/WAFAAS/pages/3932297/Bot%2BProtection)) That page outlines various bot mitigation controls and crawler handling options. Read the page directly for the current setting names, because hosted consoles change faster than blog posts.

A short, plain-language reading of each:

- **Honeypots:** hidden traps that a real visitor never triggers and a naive crawler may follow. They produce evidence, and they are cheap to test because they do not touch real-user paths.
- **Client challenges:** a check issued to the client before the request proceeds. Challenges add friction, so apply them to specific routes (login, search, checkout) and not the whole site.
- **Predefined and allowed bots:** a list of known bot types and a way to permit the ones you want. Your allow list is policy. Decide it before the first test.
- **AI crawlers:** a category for AI-related crawlers. Decide per crawler whether you allow, challenge or block, and write down why.

Then the commercial question. The technical page does not say which of these controls come with which hosted plan, or whether any of it is a separate license. Put it on the list for Barracuda: confirm which plan includes each control, in writing, before you sign. Do not accept a verbal "it's included."

## Safe evaluation steps: monitor first, baseline, verify crawlers, test only what you own

A bot control that blocks your best customers is worse than no control. Run the evaluation in this order, and keep a log of observed results at every step.

1. **Monitor first.** Start in a non-blocking mode wherever the product offers one. Collect classification data for at least a full business cycle, including your busiest day, before you change an action.
2. **Baseline real users.** Record completion rates for the routes you care about (login, checkout, paywall, search) before any enforcement. Success is the same completion rate after enforcement, not a bigger blocked count. Our guide to [bot false positive testing](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/bot-false-positive-testing-verify-visitors-before-blocking) walks through verifying visitors before blocking.
3. **Verify approved crawlers by IP and reverse DNS.** Never trust a user agent string alone. For each crawler you intend to allow, check the source IP against the operator's published ranges where they exist. Then confirm with a reverse DNS lookup followed by a forward lookup that resolves back to the same IP. Spoofed crawler names are common, so an allow rule keyed on the name alone is an open door.
4. **Run only authorized scraping tests.** Test against properties you own or have written permission to test. Use a handful of tools, including a plain HTTP client and a real headless browser, and run scripted multi-request sessions, since the dashboard documentation describes classification over multiple requests.
5. **Log observed results.** For each test, record the date, tool, route, source network, the action taken and the dashboard classification. Note misses as carefully as catches.

Don't promise yourself an outcome in advance. The output of this plan is your own measured numbers, and those are the only evidence worth taking into a contract discussion.

## Where Centinel fits beside your existing CDN or edge

Centinel Analytica is bot and AI crawler protection that tells real visitors from scrapers that look like them. It applies allow, challenge or block policy through your existing CDN or edge. It works alongside Cloudflare, CloudFront, Akamai and Fastly, and your CDN or WAF stays in place. ([Centinel Analytica](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/))

If you run Barracuda in front of your application, the useful conversation is about policy, not plumbing. Which traffic do you allow (verified crawlers, partners), which do you challenge (unknown clients on sensitive routes), and which do you block (confirmed scrapers)? Writing that three-way policy down first makes any product easier to evaluate, ours included.

Name-based allow lists often fail in practice, as requests claiming to be legitimate crawlers like GPTBot can easily be spoofed. Verify by evidence, not by label.

For how other vendors' controls are structured, read our guides to [Imperva Advanced Bot Protection](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/imperva-advanced-bot-protection-controls-and-limits) and [Cequence bot protection](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/cequence-bot-protection-deployment-and-policy-checks).

## Questions to send Barracuda before you sign

Send these in writing and file the answers with the contract. Each one targets a gap that the three documentation pages leave open.

- Which deployment am I buying (appliance or WAF-as-a-Service), and which documentation page describes each feature I expect to use?
- Is ABP a separate license on the appliance, and what exactly does my entitlement unlock?
- Which cloud components does the appliance feature depend on, and what network access do they need?

- How do I roll back a control quickly if real users are affected?
- Which behavior differs between the appliance and the hosted service, in writing?

Anything Barracuda cannot answer with a page reference goes in your risk register as unconfirmed.

## Conclusion

Treat the licensing question and the testing question as one project. Settle which deployment you are buying, get each feature tied to a documentation page, then run the monitor-first plan above and keep your own logs.

Decide with measured results, not with a feature list.
