# Cequence Bot Protection: Deployment and Policy Checks

Cequence bot protection evaluated from public evidence: what Defender with Istio and Envoy shows, which claims to attribute, and a test plan for your pilot.

By Centinel Analytica. Published 2026-11-03.

A vendor diagram is not a request path. That sounds obvious until a pilot starts and three people in the room are each picturing a different architecture: one sees a CDN plugin, one sees an inline proxy, one sees an API sidecar. All three can find a Cequence slide that supports their picture.

This article is for the platform engineers, security leads and CTOs at publishers and ecommerce companies who are evaluating or already piloting cequence bot protection. It is not a ranking. It separates what Cequence's current public documentation shows from what appears in a June 2026 announcement, a 2020 Fastly PDF and features that depend on your contract. Then it gives you a repeatable test plan.

One caveat on method. We do not operate Cequence, and we have not tested it. Everything below about Cequence is attributed to a public source type, and anything we could not tie to current documentation is labeled as a question for your vendor call. Your pilot environment is the authority, not this post.

## Short answer: what the public evidence supports

The strongest public evidence describes Cequence Defender running inline, in the request path, alongside Istio and Envoy. That is a concrete architecture you can test. Traffic crosses a proxy tier, a decision is made there, and the result is enforced or logged at that tier.

The weaker evidence is everything else. Older integration documents show an earlier integration picture. A June 22–23, 2026 announcement announces Intent Graph and Biometric Check. Some capabilities are described as depending on your contract or package. None of those three should be treated as proof of what your deployment will do on day one.

Our position: current documentation is the baseline, and everything else is a claim with a source. Write the claim down with its source before the pilot starts. If a feature matters to your decision, it has to survive a test in your environment. A slide doesn't count.

Three questions settle most of the ambiguity:

1. Where does the decision happen: at your CDN, in your cluster, or in a Cequence-operated tier?
2. What happens to a request when that component is slow or unreachable?
3. Can you reconstruct, from logs you own, why a specific request was allowed, challenged or blocked?

The rest of this post is a way to get written answers to those three.

## What current documentation shows: Defender inline with Istio and Envoy

Cequence's public documentation describes Defender as an inline component integrated with Istio and Envoy. In practice the enforcement point is a proxy tier you may already run, or one you will need to run.

Check that against your own stack first. If your origin sits behind a managed CDN and a handful of VMs, ask what the inline deployment looks like for you. "Inline with Istio and Envoy" describes a service mesh. It says nothing about your CDN.

What an inline model gives you, in principle:

- The decision point sits on the request path, so enforcement can happen before the application sees the request.
- Latency and availability of the decision component become part of your own SLO.
- Header and body inspection depends on where TLS terminates relative to the proxy.

What it costs you:

- A new dependency in the hot path of every protected route.
- Operational ownership of version upgrades, configuration rollout and capacity.
- A need to know which client IP the component actually sees. If a CDN sits in front, the direct peer is the CDN, and the real client address arrives in forwarded headers that must be trusted only from known proxies.

Write down, in your pilot plan, the exact hop where Defender sits. Name the load balancer, the ingress, the Envoy listener and the upstream cluster. If the vendor can't name those hops for your environment, you don't have a deployment design yet.

## Old diagrams versus current availability: the 2020 Fastly PDF and contract-dependent features

A 2020 PDF describing a Fastly integration is a historical artifact. It may describe a pattern that worked then, a design intent, or a pattern that has since changed. A six-year-old diagram can't tell you which, and neither can we.

The rule is simple. A diagram older than your last two infrastructure changes is a question, not an answer. If you run Fastly, ask Cequence in writing whether the integration shown in that PDF is available today, who supports it, which Fastly products it assumes (VCL, Compute, or neither), and whether it needs a separate commercial package.

The same logic applies to contract-dependent features. A capability can be real and still not be in your order form. Before the pilot, build a list with three columns: feature, source (current docs, announcement, sales call, PDF), and contract status (included, add-on, roadmap, unknown). Any row with "unknown" in the last column is a risk you carry into the evaluation.

This isn't a Cequence-specific problem. Every bot management vendor has features that live in marketing before they live in your tenant. We made the same point in our guide to [Cloudflare bot protection pricing and the enterprise quote checklist](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/cloudflare-bot-protection-pricing-enterprise-quote-checklist), and we covered the CDN-side version for [Fastly bot protection with pre-cache and post-cache checks](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/fastly-bot-protection-pre-cache-and-post-cache-checks). Where a check runs relative to the cache changes what it can see and what it costs you per request.

Ask for a dated statement of support. "Works with Fastly" is a slogan. "Version X, product Y, supported as of date Z" is something you can hold the vendor to.

## Marketing claims to attribute, not adopt: Intent Graph and Biometric Check

The June 2026 announcement introduces names such as Intent Graph and Biometric Check. We won't describe how those work. We have no public documentation that explains their mechanics, and inventing an explanation would be worse than saying nothing.

What you should do is attribute them correctly. In your evaluation notes, write "Cequence announcement, June 2026, describes a capability called Intent Graph." Don't write "Cequence detects intent." The first sentence is a fact about a document. The second is a performance claim you haven't verified.

For each named feature, get answers to five questions before it influences your decision:

1. Is it generally available today, or announced?
2. Which deployment modes support it (inline Defender, API-based, CDN-integrated)?
3. What data does it need from the browser or client, and does that require a script on your pages?
4. What does it emit into your logs, and in what fields?
5. How is it priced and is it in your contract?

A name like "Biometric Check" also carries a privacy question. If it implies collecting behavioral or device signals from visitors, your legal and privacy teams need to know what is collected, where it is stored and under which lawful basis. Ask before the pilot touches production traffic, not after.

A good rule for any vendor, ours included: a feature name is a label, not evidence. Evidence is a test result you can reproduce.

## Deployment checks: request path, enforcement location, timeouts and fail behavior

Four checks decide whether an inline bot layer is safe to put in front of revenue pages. Run them in staging first, then on a low-risk production route.

**1. Request path.** Draw the path with real hostnames. Client, CDN, load balancer, ingress, Envoy, Defender, application. Confirm each hop by sending a request with a unique header and finding it in the logs of every tier. If a hop doesn't show the marker, it isn't where you think it is.

**2. Enforcement location.** A decision can be made in one place and enforced in another. Find out which. If the decision happens in your cluster but your CDN has already cached the page, a blocked client may still be served from cache. Test with a cacheable URL and an uncacheable one.

**3. Timeouts.** Ask for the default timeout the proxy applies when waiting on the decision component. Then measure it. Add artificial latency to the decision path in staging and record the p50, p95 and p99 effect on page response time. A decision budget of tens of milliseconds can turn into seconds when something degrades.

**4. Fail behavior.** This is the most important line in the whole evaluation. When the decision component is unreachable, does the request fail open (served without a decision) or fail closed (rejected)? For a news site during a breaking story, fail closed can be an outage. For a checkout during a sneaker drop, fail open can be an attack window. Pick the behavior per route, and verify it by actually stopping the component in staging.

Our post on [Nginx bot protection and safe rollout](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/nginx-bot-protection-rate-limits-real-ips-and-safe-rollout) covers the real-IP and trusted-proxy side of this in more detail. The same trusted-proxy discipline applies to Envoy.

## Logging and policy checks: what you must be able to reconstruct

If you can't reconstruct a decision, you can't defend it to a customer, a partner or an auditor. Set the bar before you sign: for any single request, your team must be able to answer six questions from logs you can export.

1. What did the client claim to be (user agent, declared identity)?
2. What source address did the enforcement point see, and was that the real client or a proxy?
3. Which policy matched, by name and version?
4. What action was taken: allow, challenge, block, or monitor-only?
5. What evidence or score drove the match, in a field you can read?
6. What did the visitor experience afterwards, such as a challenge pass, a completed checkout or a retry?

Most pilots skip the sixth question. Blocking counts are not success. Completed legitimate sessions are. Our guide to [bot false positive testing](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/bot-false-positive-testing-verify-visitors-before-blocking) lays out how to track both sides.

On policy, require these capabilities in writing:

- A monitor-only mode per policy, so you can observe before enforcing.
- Per-route and per-hostname scoping, so a rule for login doesn't touch article pages.
- Allow-listing for crawlers you have approved, verified by more than the user agent string.
- Versioned policy changes with an audit trail and rollback.
- Log export to your own SIEM or object store, with retention you control.

Ask to see a real log line, not a dashboard screenshot. A dashboard summarizes. A log line proves.

## Repeatable authorized tests with ordinary users and automation

Run these only against systems you own or have written permission to test, and tell your security and operations teams before you start. The goal is a test matrix you can rerun after every policy change.

**Ordinary-user baseline.** Recruit a small group on different networks and devices: corporate laptop, home broadband, mobile data, a privacy-focused browser, a VPN user and someone using a screen reader. Have them complete the journeys that earn money: read an article past a meter, log in, add to cart, check out. Record any challenge, delay or block. This group is your false-positive canary.

**Simple automation.** Use your own scripted HTTP client with a default library user agent against a protected route. Then set the same client's user agent to a common browser string. Record whether the action differs, and what the logs show for each.

**Browser automation.** Run a standard headless browser setup that you control against a staging route. Capture the outcome. Then repeat with the settings your own QA team uses for regression tests, because those must keep working. Approved automation needs an explicit allow path.

**Declared crawler claims.** Send a request from an address you control that claims a well-known crawler name. A claim is not proof, and your policy should treat it that way. For background on why, see our notes on [what ClaudeBot is and how its traffic is identified](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/what-is-claudebot-anthropics-crawler-explained).

**Failure drills.** Stop the decision component in staging and watch what the proxy does. Restore it and confirm it recovers without a manual step.

Save inputs, timestamps and outputs for every run. A test you can't repeat in a month is an anecdote.

## Where an add-on layer beside your CDN fits (Centinel allow, challenge, block) and questions for your vendor call

Some teams don't want a new inline tier in their cluster. They want to keep the CDN or WAF they already run and add a layer that decides who gets through. That is where Centinel Analytica sits. It tells real visitors from scrapers and applies allow, challenge or block policy through your existing CDN or edge.

The evaluation logic in this post applies to us as much as to anyone. Ask us for the request path, the enforcement point and the log fields, and test them the same way. Our published research shows the kind of evidence to ask any vendor for. On a typical news site, 84% of requests claiming to be GPTBot were fake, so a crawler name in a user agent is not an identity.

Questions for your Cequence call, in order:

1. Which exact deployment mode applies to our stack, and which public document describes it?
2. Is the integration shown in the 2020 Fastly PDF supported today? Since when, and by whom?
3. Which announced features, including Intent Graph and Biometric Check, are generally available in our contract?
4. What is the default timeout, and is fail-open or fail-closed configurable per route?
5. Which log fields show the matched policy and the evidence behind it, and can we export them?
6. What does a rollback look like, and how long does it take?

Get the answers by email. Verbal answers don't survive a staff change.

## Conclusion

Don't sign off on cequence bot protection, or any bot layer, until you hold a one-page document with the request path, the enforcement point, the fail behavior per route and a sample log line, each tied to a dated source. If the vendor can't fill that page, the pilot isn't ready, whatever the announcement said.

If you'd rather add a decision layer beside the CDN you already run than a new inline tier, run the same checklist against Centinel Analytica. Bring both reports to your next vendor call.

# Bytespider Bot Attack: Diagnose and Contain Crawler Load

Seeing a Bytespider bot attack in your logs? Prove impact first, treat the user-agent as a claim, scope blocks narrowly, and confirm origin and readers recovered.

By Centinel Analytica. Published 2026-11-03.

At 02:40 on a Tuesday, the on-call engineer at a mid-size publisher opens the CDN dashboard and sees one user-agent string dominating the top-talkers list: Bytespider. The Slack channel fills up with the word "attack" within minutes. Someone proposes a blanket block. Someone else asks whether blocking will hurt the SEO team's crawl budget. Nobody has yet answered the first question: is anything actually broken?

Any crawler with a reputation for heavy request volume quickly triggers concern. That reputation is exactly why a spike carrying its name triggers a reflex. The reflex skips three steps: proving that the load hurt readers or the origin, checking whether the label is even true, and choosing a response small enough to reverse.

This guide walks through the incident in that order. It's written for platform engineers, SREs and security leads who sit behind Cloudflare or another CDN and need a defensible decision, not a gut call. The goal is a containment you can explain in the postmortem and a recovery you can measure.

## A Bytespider label is a claim, not a diagnosis

A user-agent header is text the client chose to send. Anyone running curl can write `Bytespider` into it in four seconds. So when your dashboard groups traffic under that name, it's grouping requests that claim a name, nothing more.

That distinction matters because the label drives the story your team tells itself. "Bytespider is hammering us" sounds like a known actor with a known behavior, and it suggests a known fix. "Some clients using the Bytespider string are sending a lot of requests" is a weaker sentence, but it's the accurate one, and it keeps your options open.

Spoofed crawler names are common. Centinel's published research found that 84% of requests claiming to be GPTBot on a typical news site were fake. Those figures come from other crawler names, not Bytespider, so don't read them as a Bytespider rate. They do show how cheap the borrowed-name trick is, and that a famous name in the logs tells you little about who sent the request.

So start the incident with a rule: write the label into your notes as "claims to be Bytespider" until you have evidence for anything stronger. Keep the word "attack" out of the ticket title for now. An attack is a statement about harm and intent, and you've shown neither yet.

Three questions structure everything below. Did the traffic hurt anyone? Who is the requester behind the label? What is the smallest control that fixes the harm? Answer them in that order.

## Establish impact before you call it an attack

High request volume is a measurement. Impact is a consequence. Plenty of crawler spikes are loud on a chart and harmless to readers, and a few quiet ones drain an origin. Measure the consequence.

Pull these numbers for the spike window and for the same window one week earlier:

- Origin CPU, connection count and database query latency. Edge-served cache hits cost almost nothing, so a spike that never reaches origin is a bandwidth line item, not an outage.
- Cache hit ratio. Crawlers that walk deep archive URLs or append query strings can bypass cache and land every request on origin.
- Error rates for human-looking traffic: 5xx responses, timeouts, and slow time to first byte on your highest-value pages.
- Rendering and ad-serving delays, if your stack ties them to origin responses.
- CDN egress and request billing, which is a legitimate harm even when readers are fine.

Then make a call, and write it down. If readers saw normal latency and origin stayed under its headroom, you have a cost and policy question, not an incident. You may still decide to limit the traffic, but you can do it on a calm schedule with a robots.txt change and a rate rule, not at 3 a.m. with a block.

If origin latency climbed in step with the spike and 5xx rates rose for ordinary visitors, you have real impact, and urgency is justified. Even then, impact tells you the load is the problem. It doesn't tell you the label is honest.

A useful habit: put a one-line impact statement at the top of the incident doc, with numbers. "Origin p95 rose from 310 ms to 1.9 s between 02:35 and 03:20; cache hit ratio fell from 91% to 64%." That line decides whether you escalate, and it becomes your baseline for the recovery check later.

## Separate the claimed name from the requester: what the logs can and cannot show

Now look at who is behind the string. Your logs carry several fields, and they differ sharply in how much they can prove.

The user-agent is the weakest field, because the client writes it. The source IP is stronger, but only if you're reading the right one. Behind a CDN, the peer your server sees is the CDN edge. The client address lives in a forwarded header such as `CF-Connecting-IP` on Cloudflare, and you should trust that header only when the request arrived through your CDN's network. Check this before you build anything on IP data. A rule keyed to the edge address will either match everyone or no one.

Once you have the real client address, group the Bytespider-labelled requests by source network and ask practical questions:

- Do the addresses cluster in a small number of hosting or cloud networks, or scatter across consumer ISPs?
- Does the same address set also appear under other user-agent strings during the window?
- Does the request pattern look like a crawler (sitemap-driven, steady pacing, robots.txt fetched first) or like extraction (sequential IDs, deep pagination, no asset requests)?
- Do TLS and HTTP characteristics stay consistent across the "same" crawler, or vary from request to request?

An operator-published list of crawler IP ranges, where one exists, is a better identity check than the header. If the operator publishes nothing you can verify against, say so in your notes. Having no verification method is a finding: the name can't be confirmed from your side, and your policy has to rest on behavior and impact instead.

The logs can't show intent or ownership. A residential proxy exit, a shared office address and a real crawler all look like "an IP" in a row. Our post on [residential proxy scraper detection](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/residential-proxy-scraper-detection-how-to-test-scraping-services) covers why an address label alone proves neither a person nor a scraper.

Preserve the raw log slice before you change anything. The [scraper incident response guide](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/scraper-incident-response-preserve-evidence-before-blocking) explains why evidence disappears the moment a block takes effect.

## Scope containment: AI Crawl Control, custom rules and log-first testing

Containment should be the smallest change that removes the measured harm. Start with the gentlest tool that could work and move up only when the numbers say so.

If you run Cloudflare, its AI Crawl Control feature (per Cloudflare's documentation, which you should check for your plan) lets you see AI crawlers by name and set a policy per crawler, such as allow or block. This suits the case where the traffic really is a declared AI crawler and your question is policy: do we want this crawler on our content at all? Pair it with robots.txt, which well-behaved crawlers read. Treat robots.txt as a request, not enforcement.

For anything the crawler-level control doesn't cover, write a custom rule. Scope it to the evidence you collected:

- Match the claimed user-agent string AND the path pattern that is hurting origin (for example, archive pagination or search URLs), not the whole site.
- Prefer a rate limit or managed challenge over a hard block for the first pass. Both are easier to undo and both give you data about who responds.
- Exclude paths your real readers and approved crawlers need: article pages for search engines, feeds you syndicate, and any partner integrations.

Then test in log-only mode first. Run the rule for a day, or at least a few hours of peak traffic, and review what it would have matched. Look for surprises: legitimate monitoring tools, partner fetchers, your own staging checks. Our walkthrough on [bot false positive testing](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/bot-false-positive-testing-verify-visitors-before-blocking) shows how to verify visitors before you enforce.

Only after the log run looks clean should you flip the rule to challenge or block, and set a calendar reminder to review it. Temporary incident rules have a habit of becoming permanent, then blocking something nobody remembers. Name the rule with the incident ID and the date so the next engineer can find its reason.

## What header matching does not do: renamed scrapers and identity

Here's the uncomfortable limit of everything in the previous section: a rule that matches the string `Bytespider` stops clients that keep using that string. It stops nobody else.

A scraper that wants your content and sees itself blocked changes one header and returns. The same extraction can come back as a generic browser user-agent, from the same infrastructure, ten minutes later. Your dashboard will show the Bytespider line falling to zero and look like a win, while the origin load continues under a different name. This is the most common false ending to these incidents.

The inverse also happens. If a real crawler honors your rule and a lookalike scraper doesn't, you've blocked the cooperative actor and left the abusive one running. Header matching rewards honesty and punishes nothing else.

So watch behavior, not names, after you deploy. Track request volume to the protected paths regardless of user-agent. If total load on those paths holds steady while the labelled traffic drops, the extraction moved, and your rule only changed its costume.

This is the gap Centinel Analytica is built for. It tells real visitors from scrapers that look like them, then applies allow, challenge or block policy through your existing CDN or edge. Your Cloudflare, CloudFront, Akamai or Fastly setup stays in place. The decision rests on what the requester is, not on what it calls itself. Chasing a list of user-agent strings is the alternative, and the list is always one rename behind.

For publishers weighing what to allow and what to refuse, the [AI crawler policy template](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/ai-crawler-policy-for-publishers-a-newsroom-access-template) gives a starting structure that separates stated policy from enforcement.

## Validate recovery for readers and origin

A quiet dashboard is not recovery. Recovery means the harm you measured in the impact step is gone and nothing new broke. Check both halves.

First, compare against the baseline line you wrote at the start. Within an hour of the rule going live, you want to see origin p95 latency back near its pre-spike value, cache hit ratio recovering, and connection counts under their headroom. If the labelled traffic dropped but origin metrics didn't move, the load was never the labelled traffic, and you've been treating the wrong thing.

Second, look for collateral damage. Pull the same reader-facing numbers you used for impact: 5xx rates, challenge-solve rates if you used challenges, and bounce or session counts on article pages. A fall in sessions that tracks your rule's start time is a false positive until proven otherwise. Check your search engine crawl stats too, since an overly broad rule can quietly block the crawlers you want. Verify real Googlebot by reverse DNS, not by the user-agent string, for the same reason this whole article distrusts names.

Third, watch for displacement over the next two to three days. Extraction that moves under a new name will show up as sustained request pressure on the same URL patterns from new source networks. If you see that, your containment worked on the label and failed on the behavior, and it's time for the next tier of controls rather than another header tweak.

Close the loop with a short written verdict: impact confirmed or not, what was changed, what the metrics did afterward, and whether the rule stays, narrows or goes. A rule with no verdict is technical debt with a date on it.

## Incident notes to keep and when to escalate beyond header rules

Good notes turn a stressful night into a reusable playbook. Keep these, in this order:

- The impact statement with before and after numbers, and the exact time window.
- The raw log slice, stored outside the system you're about to change.
- The distinction between the claimed name and anything you verified about the requester, including which header you trusted for the client IP and why.
- Each rule you added: its match conditions, its action, its mode (log, challenge, block), the date, and the owner.
- What the log-only run would have matched, including any legitimate hits you excluded.
- The recovery verdict and the planned review date.

These notes are also your evidence if a partner, a legal team or an executive asks why a crawler was blocked.

Escalate beyond header and path rules when any of these hold: the load returns under a different user-agent after you contain the first one, source addresses rotate faster than you can list them, the traffic targets login, checkout or API routes where a false positive costs revenue, or the extraction is of content you license or sell. At that point you're no longer managing a named crawler. You're separating real visitors from software that imitates them, and static string rules can't do that job.

For ecommerce teams, the [price scraping protection guide](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/price-scraping-protection-test-controls-on-product-pages) shows how to test controls on product pages. For publishers, [bot mitigation for publishers](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/bot-mitigation-for-publishers-manage-unknown-crawlers-at-edge) covers handling unknown crawlers at the edge.

## Conclusion

Treat the next spike labelled Bytespider as a hypothesis to test, not a verdict to act on. Measure impact first, record the name as a claim, contain narrowly, and confirm that readers and origin recovered before you close the ticket.

If your containment ended with the Bytespider line dropping while load on the same paths stayed flat, header rules have reached their limit. Then use the 30-minute demo to look at how Centinel applies allow, challenge or block policy through the CDN you already run, based on what the requester is rather than what it calls itself.


## Frequently asked questions

### Is Bytespider traffic always a real ByteDance crawler?

No. The Bytespider name arrives in a user-agent header, and any client can type that string. Treat it as a claim until you verify the requester through an operator-published IP list or behavior. Centinel's research found 84% of GPTBot-labelled requests on a typical news site were fake, which shows how often crawler names get borrowed.

### How do I tell whether a Bytespider spike is actually hurting my site?

Compare origin CPU, database latency, cache hit ratio and reader-facing 5xx rates for the spike window against the same window a week earlier. If readers saw normal speed and origin kept headroom, it is a cost or policy issue, not an outage. Write the before and after numbers into the incident notes.

### Will blocking the Bytespider user-agent stop the scraping?

Only if the client keeps using that name. A scraper can change one header and return from the same infrastructure. After any header rule, watch total request volume on the affected paths. If it holds steady while the labelled traffic falls, the extraction moved. Centinel Analytica tells real visitors from scrapers rather than relying on the declared name.

### Should I test a bot rule before turning on a block?

Yes. Run the rule in log-only mode through a peak period and review what it would have matched, looking for partner fetchers, monitoring tools and your own checks. Then move to a challenge or rate limit before a hard block, and name the rule with the incident ID so it can be reviewed later.

### Can I add bot protection without replacing Cloudflare?

Centinel Analytica states that it works alongside Cloudflare, CloudFront, Akamai and Fastly, and that your CDN or WAF stays in place. It applies allow, challenge or block policy through your existing CDN or edge. Readers should confirm integration details for their own setup during the demo.

# Cloudflare Bot Management Alternatives: Architecture First

Compare Cloudflare Bot Management alternatives by where the decision is made and what evidence it sees, plus four acceptance tests to run on any vendor.

By Centinel Analytica. Published 2026-11-03.

Most bot protection comparisons read like grocery lists. One column says ML scoring, the next says JavaScript detections, the third says CAPTCHA alternative, and every vendor gets a green check on every row. You finish the spreadsheet knowing nothing about which product will catch the scraper that already walked through your checkout.

A better way to compare Cloudflare Bot Management alternatives is to ask two questions about each product. Where does the allow, challenge or block decision get made? And what evidence does the system see when it makes that decision: the request, the browser, the connection, or only one of them?

Those two answers explain most of the differences you will see in a bake-off. They also tell you what you have to change in your stack to adopt the product. This article walks through Cloudflare Bot Management, DataDome and Centinel on those terms, then gives you four acceptance tests (JA4 correlation, residential proxy behavior, Googlebot reverse DNS and decision latency) that you can run against any vendor, including ours. They are tests you run, not claims we make.

## Short answer: what to look for in a Cloudflare Bot Management alternative

Look for three things, in this order.

First, the decision point. A product that decides inside your CDN is fast and consolidated, but it can only judge what the CDN sees. A product that decides in your application or beside your CDN can see more context, but you own an extra hop. Neither is free. Pick the tradeoff on purpose.

Second, evidence coverage. A request-only system reads headers, IP and user agent. A browser-aware system also looks at what the client environment exposes. A connection-aware system looks at how the client negotiated TLS and HTTP. The scrapers that matter today (Playwright with stealth patches, Camoufox, hosted browser services behind residential proxies) are built to pass one layer. They rarely pass all three consistently, which is why you should judge the layers together.

Third, enforcement path. Can the vendor's verdict be applied through the CDN or proxy you already run, or does adoption mean moving DNS? If you are on Cloudflare, CloudFront, Akamai or Fastly, an add-on layer that keeps your CDN or WAF in place is a smaller migration than a replacement.

Ignore the feature checklist until those three are settled. Every vendor can claim bot scores. Few will tell you plainly which layer of evidence produced the score.

## How Cloudflare Bot Management decides: edge scoring inside the CDN

Cloudflare Bot Management evaluates traffic directly at the network edge. That is its strongest property. The verdict is computed before the request reaches your origin, and the result is exposed to your own rules, so you can write a WAF expression against a bot score and act on it in the same place you already manage traffic.

The tradeoff is that the decision is bound to the CDN. Cloudflare sees the connection and the request very well, because it is the connection. Browser-side evidence depends on its JavaScript detections being served and executed on the page. If the client never runs script, or runs a browser configured to look ordinary, the verdict leans on what the edge could observe.

There is also a packaging issue. Different protection tiers offer varying capabilities, and enterprise-grade features often require higher-level agreements. If you are comparing alternatives because the quote surprised you, our [enterprise quote checklist for Cloudflare bot protection pricing](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/cloudflare-bot-protection-pricing-enterprise-quote-checklist) lists what to ask before you sign.

Here is our position: edge scoring inside the CDN is the right default for teams that want one vendor for delivery, WAF and bots, and that accept the CDN as the boundary of the decision. It is the wrong fit when you run a multi-CDN setup, when your CDN is not Cloudflare, or when you need the bot decision to be portable. Consolidation is a real benefit. Treat it as a purchase criterion, not as proof of detection quality.

## How DataDome decides: server-side checks plus a JavaScript tag

DataDome combines server-side inspection with client-side telemetry to evaluate incoming traffic. The vendor sits beside your delivery stack rather than inside it, and it ships integrations for common CDNs and web servers.

That architecture gives it two evidence streams: the request as seen at your integration point, and the browser as seen by the tag. In practice, the first request from a new client is judged mostly on request evidence, and richer browser evidence builds up as the tag runs. A scraper that fetches a single URL once from a fresh address may never give the tag a chance to report.

So ask DataDome, and any tag-based vendor, three concrete questions. What verdict does a client get on its first request, before any tag data exists? What happens to API endpoints and non-HTML responses where no tag can run? And what happens if the integration cannot reach the vendor's decision service?

DataDome's tag-plus-server design suits sites that want an add-on layer and are comfortable shipping a script to every page. The cost is operational: one more integration to deploy per entry point, and a client-side dependency to monitor for performance and breakage. That is a fair trade for many teams. Just know you are buying a two-stage decision, and test the first stage separately from the second.

## How Centinel approaches it: request, browser and connection judged together, enforced through your existing CDN

Centinel tells real visitors from scrapers, then applies allow, challenge or block policy through your existing CDN or edge. It works alongside your existing infrastructure, allowing your CDN or WAF to stay in place. Centinel's evaluation makes the decision. Enforcement happens where you already enforce.

Evasion tools are built layer by layer. A hosted browser service can present a convincing browser environment while its connection characteristics still look like an automation stack. A residential proxy can give a request a consumer IP while the client behind it behaves nothing like a consumer browser. A fake crawler can send a perfect user agent string while failing every other check. Score the layers in isolation and each one can be satisfied. Compare them against each other and the mismatch is the signal.

Our background shapes the approach. We have spent significant time testing scraping tools against various detection mechanisms to see where protection holds and where it fails. We also published fake-crawler research: on a typical news site, 84% of requests claiming to be GPTBot were fake. That number is why we do not treat a declared crawler name as evidence of anything.

If you are on Fastly and wondering how an add-on layer fits around caching, our post on [Fastly bot protection and pre-cache versus post-cache checks](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/fastly-bot-protection-pre-cache-and-post-cache-checks) covers where the check should sit.

## Four acceptance tests to run on any vendor

Do not accept a vendor's description of its own detection. Run these four tests in your bake-off, on Cloudflare, DataDome, Centinel and anyone else on the shortlist. Each one is something you verify, not something we promise.

**1. JA4 correlation.** JA4 is a TLS client fingerprint format from FoxIO. Capture the JA4 of a real Chrome session and of the same scraping tool you plan to test (Playwright, Camoufox, a curl-impersonation library). Then ask the vendor to show you, in logs or the dashboard, whether the connection fingerprint was compared against the claimed user agent and browser environment. A pass is a visible mismatch verdict when a Chrome user agent arrives on a non-Chrome handshake. A fail is a verdict that never mentions the connection.

**2. Residential proxy behavior.** Route a scripted client through a residential proxy service you pay for. Run it against a protected page and a protected action, such as search, login or add to cart. Record whether each request was allowed, challenged or blocked, and on what stated evidence. IP reputation alone should not decide this test. Our guide on [testing scraping services behind residential proxies](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/residential-proxy-scraper-detection-how-to-test-scraping-services) gives a method.

**3. Googlebot reverse DNS.** Send requests claiming to be Googlebot from an address that is not Google's. Then confirm that real Googlebot, verified by reverse DNS lookup followed by a forward lookup that returns the same IP (Google's documented method), is still allowed. A vendor has to block the impostor and pass the real crawler, or your search traffic pays for the test.

**4. Decision latency.** Measure added latency at your own p50 and p99 with the vendor in the path, on a cache hit and a cache miss, from the regions your readers use. Set your threshold before the test. Many teams use a figure in the low single-digit milliseconds for inline decisions. Whatever number you pick, measure it yourself and write it into the contract language.

## Choosing by architecture: CDN consolidation vs add-on layer, and a bake-off plan

Here is the decision rule. If your priority is one vendor, one dashboard and one invoice, and you are happy being on Cloudflare for the long run, stay with Cloudflare Bot Management and negotiate the tier. If your CDN is not Cloudflare, or you expect it to change, an add-on layer keeps the bot decision independent of the delivery decision. That independence has a price (an extra integration) and a payoff (portability).

Between add-on layers, choose by evidence. A tag-based design makes sense when most of your value is in HTML pages and you can ship script everywhere. A design that judges request, browser and connection together makes sense when your problem includes APIs, headless browsers behind residential proxies, and fake crawlers.

Run the bake-off in four steps:

1. Pick two protected routes: one content route (article or product page) and one interactive route (login, checkout or search).
2. Run in monitor mode for two weeks on production traffic. Log what each vendor would have done. Do not enforce yet.
3. Execute the four acceptance tests above against each vendor, with the same tools and the same proxy provider.
4. Review false positives before any enforcement. Our post on [bot false positive testing](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/bot-false-positive-testing-verify-visitors-before-blocking) shows how to verify visitors before you block them.

Decide on the evidence in your own logs, not on the demo.

## Conclusion

Pick your Cloudflare Bot Management alternative by architecture, then prove it with your own traffic. If you already run Cloudflare, CloudFront, Akamai or Fastly and want bot protection without replacing your CDN, put Centinel on your shortlist. Then book the 30-minute demo and bring the four acceptance tests. Ask us to show the JA4 mismatch, the residential proxy run, the Googlebot reverse DNS check and the latency numbers on your own routes. If a vendor can't pass them in your environment, the feature checklist doesn't matter.


## Frequently asked questions

### What are the best Cloudflare Bot Management alternatives?

The common alternatives are add-on bot protection layers such as DataDome and Centinel, plus the bot products from Akamai, HUMAN Security and Kasada. Choose by where the decision is made and which evidence it sees. Centinel tells real visitors from scrapers and enforces through your existing CDN.

### Can I use bot protection alongside Cloudflare instead of replacing it?

Yes. Centinel states that it works alongside Cloudflare, CloudFront, Akamai and Fastly, and that your CDN or WAF stays in place. It applies allow, challenge or block policy through your existing CDN or edge. Verify the integration path for your setup during a demo.

### How do I test whether a bot management vendor catches fake Googlebot traffic?

Send requests claiming to be Googlebot from a non-Google IP and confirm they are blocked or challenged. Then confirm real Googlebot, verified by reverse DNS plus a matching forward lookup, is still allowed.

### What is JA4 and why does it matter when comparing bot protection?

JA4 is a TLS client fingerprint format from FoxIO. It describes how a client negotiates its connection. Comparing it against the claimed user agent can expose automation tools that spoof a browser. Run it as an acceptance test on every vendor and ask to see the mismatch in logs.

### How much latency should bot detection add to a request?

Set your own threshold, then measure it. Test p50 and p99 on cache hits and misses from your readers' regions with the vendor in the path. Many teams target low single-digit milliseconds for inline decisions. Treat any figure as something to verify in your bake-off, not a vendor promise.

# Ecommerce Bot Protection: Prevent Inventory Hoarding

Ecommerce bot protection for inventory hoarding: map where add-to-cart reserves stock, cap unpaid holds, and test how much stock sits held but unpaid.

By Centinel Analytica. Published 2026-10-31.

A retailer launches a limited sneaker drop at noon. By 12:03 the product page shows "sold out." By 12:20 it is back in stock, then gone again at 12:21. Orders paid for in that window: a fraction of the units that vanished. The rest sat in carts that nobody intended to pay for, held by sessions that renewed the hold every few minutes.

This is inventory hoarding, and it is a different problem from scalping or card testing. The bot does not want to buy. It wants real shoppers to be unable to. OWASP classifies the behavior as OAT-021, Denial of Inventory, in its Automated Threats to Web Applications handbook (OWASP, 2015).

Most bot guides skip the first engineering question: does add-to-cart reserve stock in your store at all? If it does not, hoarding is mostly a nuisance. If it does, every cart is a lock on revenue. This post walks through where the hold begins, how it expires, where bots exploit renewal, what the logs look like, and which application controls cap the damage before you ever reach for ecommerce bot protection at the edge.

## Denial of inventory vs scalping vs card testing: what this post covers

Three bot problems get lumped together under checkout fraud. They need different fixes, so separate them first.

**Scalping** (OWASP OAT-005) means obtaining limited-availability or preferred goods or services by unfair methods, such as buying scarce items to resell. The bot completes payment. Your inventory count is accurate, you just sold to the wrong party. **Card testing** (OAT-001, carding) means running stolen card numbers through your payment step to see which ones work. It hits your payment endpoint and your processor fees. **Denial of inventory** (OAT-021) means holding stock without paying. The bot adds items to carts or starts checkouts and never finishes.

The tell is the conversion shape. Scalping shows high paid conversion from odd buyers. Card testing shows many small payment attempts with high decline rates. Denial of inventory shows a high rate of carts, reservations or checkout starts that expire unpaid, often with a suspiciously regular rhythm.

This post covers only the third. It is also not a general abandoned-cart guide. Real shoppers abandon carts constantly, and a reservation system has to tolerate that. The goal is to cap how much stock any one actor can tie up, and to make sure bots cannot do it at scale for free.

If your concern is the payment side, the post on [checkout fraud detection](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/checkout-fraud-detection-separate-bot-traffic-from-payment-risk) separates bot traffic from payment risk. Come back here when the symptom is stock that disappears and does not convert.

## Does add-to-cart reserve stock in your store? Map where reservation begins

Don't assume. Platforms differ, and customizations differ more. There are four common reservation points, and your store may use more than one.

1. **No reservation until payment.** Add-to-cart only records intent. Stock decrements when the order is placed or the payment is captured. Hoarding through carts does nothing to availability, though it can still distort analytics and waste server work.
2. **Reservation at add-to-cart.** The cart line item decrements available quantity or creates a hold record. This is the most exposed design, because the cheapest action (one POST) takes stock.
3. **Reservation at checkout start.** Stock is held when the shopper enters the checkout flow or submits shipping details. Slightly harder to automate, still scriptable.
4. **Reservation at payment authorization.** Stock is held while the payment is pending, typically for minutes. The window is narrow, but a bot can open many pending authorizations.

To map yours, do this today. Pick a product with a stock of three. Add two units to a cart in one browser, then check availability from a second browser with no session. Note when availability changes. Repeat after beginning checkout, and again after entering payment details without submitting.

Then read the code or the platform configuration that owns the decrement. Look for a hold table, a reservation service, a database column such as reserved_quantity, or an inventory API call made from the cart controller. Write down the exact endpoint that creates the hold and who is allowed to call it.

That endpoint is your protected route. Everything later in this post attaches to it.

## How holds are created, expired and renewed (and where bots exploit renewal)

A hold has three lifecycle events: creation, expiry and renewal. Bots abuse the third.

**Creation** needs a quantity, a product or variant identifier, and an owner. The owner is a session ID, a cart token or a customer account. Check how cheaply an owner can be minted. If a fresh anonymous session can create a hold with one unauthenticated request, a script can mint thousands of owners.

**Expiry** is usually a timer: 10, 15 or 30 minutes from creation. Check where the timer lives. A TTL on a Redis key expires reliably. A scheduled job that sweeps expired holds every hour does not, and stock stays locked until the next sweep. Also check what happens on a failed sweep. A hold with no working expiry is a permanent lock.

**Renewal** is where designs leak. Common renewal triggers include any cart update, any page view that touches the cart, a checkout step transition, and a payment retry. If viewing the cart page resets the timer, a bot that polls the cart every 9 minutes holds stock indefinitely with trivial traffic. The same applies to quantity edits: change 2 to 3 to 2, and the clock restarts.

Two patterns show up repeatedly in abuse. The first is **renewal polling**: a low-rate request on a fixed interval just under the TTL. The second is **session rotation**: when a hold nears its cap, the script creates a new session and re-adds the item, so no single owner looks greedy.

Fix renewal at the design level. Make the TTL absolute from creation, or allow a limited number of renewals (for example, one extension tied to a real checkout step). Renewal should require progress toward payment, not mere presence.

## Abandoned shopping vs coordinated reservation abuse: what to look for in logs

You can't cap what you can't see. Start with the hold records or the cart and checkout endpoint logs, and look for shape rather than volume.

**Human abandonment** is messy. Hold durations vary widely. Many carts include several products. Sessions load images, scripts and other pages. Adds cluster around normal browsing hours. A fraction convert, and the ones that don't simply expire at the TTL or earlier.

**Coordinated abuse** is tidy. Look for these patterns in the logs:

- **Expiry-to-re-add gaps near zero.** The same product re-added seconds after a hold expires, from a new session.
- **Single-SKU focus.** Sessions that touch only the constrained product, with no browsing history.
- **Maximum quantity every time.** Every add uses the per-order limit.
- **Fixed renewal intervals.** Cart reads or updates at near-identical spacing.
- **Zero paid conversion across a cluster.** Group by whatever is stable (account, payment fingerprint, shipping postcode, request headers) and compare cart-to-paid ratios.
- **Missing downstream steps.** Holds created without the usual preceding page requests or asset loads.

Here's a worked comparison. Take the last constrained drop and compute, for each hold, its lifetime and whether it converted. If 70 percent of held units came from owners with a lifetime paid-conversion of zero, you have either hoarding or a very unusual customer base. Cross-check by owner count: a handful of IP addresses or ASNs behind thousands of owners is a strong signal, though residential proxies can blur it. For that case, the guide on [residential proxy scraper detection](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/residential-proxy-scraper-detection-how-to-test-scraping-services) covers why address-based grouping fails and what to compare instead.

Keep the raw evidence before you block anything. The checklist in [scraper incident response](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/scraper-incident-response-preserve-evidence-before-blocking) applies equally to hoarding incidents.

## Application controls that cap stock tied up without purchase

Application controls bound the damage even when detection is imperfect. They should work with zero bot intelligence, because bots will eventually evade detection. Build them in this order.

**1. Cap held units per owner and per product.** For a limited-stock item, set a per-owner ceiling (often one or two units) and enforce it server-side at hold creation. The cap must apply across the owner's active carts, not per cart.

**2. Cap unpaid stock as a share of available inventory.** Most stores lack this control. Define a ceiling on total held-but-unpaid units for a constrained SKU, for example 30 percent of remaining stock. When the ceiling is hit, new holds queue or fail gracefully instead of draining the shelf. Pick the percentage from your normal conversion data, and tune it per drop.

**3. Shorten and harden the TTL.** For scarce items, hold times of 5 to 10 minutes reduce exposure. Make the expiry authoritative (a database timestamp checked at read, not only a sweeper job).

**4. Limit renewals.** Allow zero or one extension, and tie it to a verifiable step such as entering a shipping address or starting payment authorization.

**5. Move the hold later for hot items.** Reserve at checkout start or payment authorization instead of add-to-cart. The tradeoff: shoppers may reach payment and find the item gone, so show availability honestly and consider a short waiting room for drops.

**6. Rate limit hold creation per session, account and network, and require an account or verified contact for constrained SKUs.** Rate limits alone are weak against rotating sessions, so treat them as a floor.

**7. Release on signals.** Release holds immediately when payment fails repeatedly, when an account is flagged, or when an owner exceeds its cap.

The edge-specific rate-limit mechanics differ by stack. See the posts on [Shopify bot protection](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/shopify-bot-protection-checkout-controls-and-storefront-limits) and [Nginx bot protection](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/nginx-bot-protection-rate-limits-real-ips-and-safe-rollout) for platform and proxy details.

## Where bot detection fits: challenge and block at the cart and reserve endpoints

Application caps limit how much a bot can take. Bot detection decides whether the request deserves to reach the cap at all. You need both.

Apply detection to the narrow set of endpoints you mapped earlier: the add-to-cart call, the reservation or checkout-start call, and any cart-read route that renews a hold. Don't run the heaviest policy sitewide. Product pages and search need to stay fast and open for legitimate crawlers and shoppers. The cart and reserve endpoints are low-traffic, high-value, and rarely hit by anyone you want to keep out.

A workable policy shape: allow requests that present consistent evidence of a real browser session, challenge ambiguous ones before the hold is created, and block the ones that clearly fail. The challenge belongs before the stock decrement, not after, because a hold created and then challenged still removed inventory.

This is where Centinel Analytica fits. It tells real visitors from scrapers that look like them and applies allow, challenge or block policy through your existing CDN or edge, so your Cloudflare, CloudFront, Akamai or Fastly setup stays in place. You point the policy at the cart and reserve routes and leave the catalog open. The team behind it are former bot builders and reverse engineers, which matters here: scripted hoarding tools imitate browsers, and detection that looks at the request, browser and connection together is harder to sidestep than a single header check.

Keep a legitimate-user escape path. A challenge on the reserve endpoint should let real shoppers retry, and you should measure the effect on genuine checkouts. The post on [bot false positive testing](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/bot-false-positive-testing-verify-visitors-before-blocking) lays out how to verify visitors before you enforce.

## Test the fix: a checklist for measuring held-but-unpaid inventory

A control you can't measure is a hope. Before and after any change, record the same numbers.

**Baseline metrics (per constrained SKU, per drop):**

- Peak held-but-unpaid units as a percentage of starting stock.
- Hold-to-paid conversion rate, by hold count and by unit count.
- Median and 95th percentile hold lifetime.
- Share of held units from owners with zero paid orders.
- Time from "sold out" display to first restock event.
- Number of renewals per hold, and the share of holds renewed more than once.

**Test steps:**

1. **Replay the previous drop's logs** against the new caps in a staging environment, and compare what the shelf would have shown.
2. **Run a synthetic hoarder.** Script a test client in your own environment that creates holds, polls to renew, and rotates sessions. Confirm each cap triggers: per-owner, per-SKU unpaid ceiling, renewal limit, and rate limit.
3. **Verify expiry under failure.** Stop the sweeper or queue worker and confirm holds still expire at read time.
4. **Check the legitimate path.** A real tester should complete a purchase during the same window with the policies on, including from a mobile network.
5. **Run in observe mode first.** Log what the challenge or block policy would have done before enforcing, and review the false-positive sample.
6. **Watch the next real drop** with a live dashboard on the metrics above and a rollback switch for each control.

Success means the unpaid share stays under your ceiling, hold lifetimes cluster at or below the TTL, and genuine conversion does not fall. If conversion falls, loosen the last control you added, not all of them.

## Conclusion

Inventory hoarding is an engineering defect first and a bot problem second. If add-to-cart takes stock, renewal never expires, and anonymous sessions cost nothing, any script can empty your shelf at noon. Fix the hold lifecycle, cap unpaid stock per owner and per SKU, then put detection in front of the cart and reserve routes. Nobody should call it solved until the held-but-unpaid metric stays flat through a real drop.

If you want to see what is hitting those routes today, Centinel Analytica can help you scope allow, challenge and block policy for your cart and reserve endpoints on top of your current CDN.


## Frequently asked questions

### What is inventory hoarding in ecommerce?

Inventory hoarding, classified by OWASP as OAT-021 Denial of Inventory, is when bots hold limited stock or availability—such as by adding items to carts—without completing the purchase or committing to the transaction. Real shoppers then see products as unavailable. It differs from scalping, where the bot completes the purchase, and from card testing, which targets the payment step.

### How do I know if bots are reserving my stock?

First confirm that add-to-cart or checkout actually holds stock in your store. Then look in hold and cart logs for near-zero gaps between expiry and re-add, fixed-interval renewals, maximum quantities on every add, single-SKU sessions, and clusters with zero paid conversion. Keep raw logs before blocking anything.

### How long should a cart hold last on a limited-stock product?

There is no universal number. For scarce items many stores use roughly 5 to 15 minutes, with an absolute expiry from creation and at most one renewal tied to real progress such as starting payment. Tune it from your own conversion data and verify the expiry still works if background jobs fail.

### Can rate limiting alone stop inventory hoarding?

Rate limits help but are not enough, because scripts rotate sessions and addresses to stay under per-owner thresholds. Pair them with server-side caps on held units, a ceiling on unpaid stock per SKU, limited renewals, and bot detection on the cart and reserve endpoints. [Centinel Analytica](https://centinelanalytica.com/bot-management) applies allow, challenge or block policy through your existing CDN.

### Where should I put bot challenges in the checkout flow?

Place them on the endpoints that create or renew a hold: add-to-cart, reservation or checkout start, and cart reads that reset timers. Challenge before the stock decrement, since a hold created then challenged already removed inventory. Leave product pages and catalog routes open, and test the effect on genuine buyers first.

# reCAPTCHA vs Cloudflare Turnstile: Server-Side Checks

A recaptcha vs cloudflare comparison from the endpoint's side: what each server response returns, which fields to check, token replay, and what to measure.

By Centinel Analytica. Published 2026-10-31.

A signup form passes its CAPTCHA check on Monday and still floods your database with junk accounts by Wednesday. The widget worked. The server-side wiring did not. That gap is where most real failures live, and it is the reason a recaptcha vs cloudflare decision should be made at the endpoint, not on the marketing page.

This post compares Google reCAPTCHA and Cloudflare Turnstile as two token-verification services that your backend calls. It does not compare Cloudflare's WAF or Bot Management, and it does not crown a winner. You will see what each verification response tells your code, which fields deserve a strict check, how tokens expire and get replayed, why one passed widget does not cover later requests, and how to measure whether legitimate people still finish the action you protect. Field names and limits below come from each vendor's public documentation, so confirm them against the current docs before you ship.

## What this compares: reCAPTCHA and Turnstile, not Cloudflare WAF or Bot Management

Keep the scope narrow, because the two products get confused with their parent companies. Turnstile is Cloudflare's CAPTCHA alternative. reCAPTCHA is Google's. Each one puts a widget or script in the browser, gets a token, and expects your server to send that token to a verification endpoint. That loop is the whole comparison here.

Cloudflare's WAF rules and Bot Management are separate products with separate configuration, billing and signals. You can run Turnstile on a site that is not proxied by Cloudflare, and you can run reCAPTCHA behind Cloudflare. Treat them as independent choices. If you only take one thing from this section: don't judge Turnstile by how you feel about Cloudflare's firewall, and don't judge reCAPTCHA by how you feel about Google's ad stack.

The decision you actually face has four parts. What does the server get back? What do you have to verify yourself? How long does a token live, and can it be reused? And what happens on the next request after the token passes?

A verification token is also not a verdict about a person. It is a short-lived claim that a browser completed a challenge or evaluation for a specific site key. Everything past that claim is your code's job. Teams that treat the pass as proof of a human, and then skip the other checks, are the teams that end up in the Monday-to-Wednesday story above.

If you have already read our notes on [form bot protection](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/form-bot-protection-reduce-fake-leads-without-blocking-buyers), this is the narrower, code-level companion to that piece.

## Two server responses: Turnstile Siteverify result vs reCAPTCHA assessment

The two services return different shapes, and that difference should drive your design.

Turnstile's server call goes to Cloudflare's Siteverify endpoint with your secret key and the token the widget produced. Cloudflare's documentation describes the response as a success boolean plus metadata such as a challenge timestamp, the hostname, an error-codes array, and the action and cdata values you set on the client. The core decision is binary: the token validated or it didn't. Your code branches on success, then inspects the metadata.

reCAPTCHA offers two server paths in Google's documentation. The classic v2 and v3 flow posts to a siteverify endpoint and receives success, a challenge timestamp, hostname, and for v3 a score and an action. The reCAPTCHA Enterprise path uses the Assessments API: you create an assessment for a token and read back a tokenProperties block (valid flag, invalid reason, hostname, action, create time) and a riskAnalysis block with a score and reason codes.

That is the real structural split. Turnstile gives you a pass or fail and asks you to apply your own policy around it. reCAPTCHA v3 and Enterprise hand you a score and expect you to pick a cutoff.

Don't invent that cutoff. Google's own guidance for v3 says to start with a default and tune from your traffic in the admin console. Log the raw score next to the outcome of each protected action, then choose a threshold from your own data. A number copied from a forum post describes someone else's traffic.

Write your handler so that an unreachable verification service is a handled state, not an exception. Decide in advance whether the endpoint fails open or closed, and write that decision down.

## Check the action and hostname before you trust a pass

A valid token only proves the challenge was solved for your site key. It doesn't prove the token was meant for this endpoint on this domain. Two fields close that gap, and both services expose them.

Hostname first. The verification response reports the hostname where the challenge ran. Compare it to an allowlist of your own domains. Without that check, a token minted on an unrelated page that shares your site key (or on a lookalike domain carrying a copied embed) can satisfy your server. Cloudflare's docs and Google's docs both describe the hostname field, and reCAPTCHA's key settings let you restrict domains, so use both layers.

Action second. reCAPTCHA v3 and Enterprise let you label each execution with an action string such as login or checkout, and the response echoes it back. Turnstile supports an action value on the widget that comes back in the Siteverify result. Pick one distinct label per endpoint, then require an exact match server-side.

Here is the before and after. Before: your /signup handler checks success and moves on, so a token generated for the newsletter box on the same site key unlocks account creation. After: /signup requires action equal to signup and hostname in your allowlist, so the newsletter token is rejected even though it is cryptographically valid.

A mismatch should be a distinct, logged rejection reason, separate from "challenge failed". When someone probes your forms, that log line is the earliest visible sign, and it is cheaper to read than a spike in chargebacks.

One more habit: never trust the action or hostname the browser reports in your own request body. Read them only from the verification response.

## Token lifetime, single use and safe retries (idempotency vs replay)

Tokens are short-lived and single-use, and that shapes your retry logic more than any other fact in this comparison.

Cloudflare's documentation states that a Turnstile token is valid for 300 seconds and can be validated only once. Google's documentation for reCAPTCHA states that a v2 response token is valid for two minutes and can be verified once, and that v3 tokens also expire after two minutes. Confirm both against the current docs, because vendors adjust these. Either way, a second verification attempt on the same token returns a failure, and an old token returns a timeout-style error code.

This creates a trap with retries. A user submits a form, your server verifies the token, then your database write times out and the client retries the same request with the same token. The second verification fails, and a legitimate user sees a rejection for something that wasn't their fault.

Separate two concerns. Replay protection stops an attacker from reusing one valid token across many requests. Idempotency lets an honest client safely repeat one request. They are different mechanisms:

- Verify the token once, at the start of the request, and record the result against an idempotency key you issue for that submission.
- On a retry carrying the same idempotency key, return the stored outcome instead of calling verification again.
- On a request with a new key but an already-used token, reject it as a replay.
- If the token has simply expired because the user left the form open, return a response that makes the client re-run the widget.

Store the token's creation time or the vendor's challenge timestamp so you can tell "expired" from "reused" in your logs. They need different fixes, and mixing them up sends you tuning the wrong control.

## Why a passed widget does not cover later authenticated requests

A passed CAPTCHA is a point-in-time event on one request. It says nothing about the next one.

Consider a login flow. The widget passes, the server verifies the token, the user gets a session cookie. From that moment, every call to your account API, cart API or export endpoint travels on the cookie, not on a CAPTCHA result. A script that obtained one valid session (by solving once, by buying access, or by taking over an account) can drive thousands of authenticated requests, and no further token check ever runs.

This is the most common misunderstanding in a recaptcha vs cloudflare evaluation. Teams ask which widget is stronger and never ask what protects the endpoints behind it. Neither product answers that. Both only vouch for the moment the token was minted.

So bind the pass to something and then bound what a session can do:

- Protect each sensitive action, not only the entry point. Password reset, address change, coupon redemption and checkout each deserve their own verified token with their own action label.
- Put rate limits and quotas on authenticated routes, keyed to the account, because changing IP addresses doesn't reset an account budget.
- Re-challenge before high-value steps such as payout changes, rather than trusting a login from hours earlier.

This is where Centinel Analytica fits next to either widget. Centinel applies allow, challenge or block policy through your existing CDN or edge, so your reCAPTCHA or Turnstile integration stays in place. The widget covers the form submission, and the policy layer covers the routes behind it. For the account-level angle, our piece on [checkout fraud detection](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/checkout-fraud-detection-separate-bot-traffic-from-payment-risk) separates bot traffic from payment risk.

## Staging tests before launch

Test the failure paths in staging, because production will find them for you at the worst time.

Both vendors publish test keys for development. Cloudflare documents dummy site keys and secret keys for Turnstile that force an always-pass, always-fail or interactive result. Use these to exercise your handler without burning real challenges, and read each vendor's docs for the current values. One caution: Cloudflare's docs note that dummy tokens only validate against the dummy secret, so a pass against a test secret says nothing about your production secret. Run one end-to-end check with real keys before launch.

Build a short checklist and run every line:

1. Valid token, right action, right hostname: request succeeds.
2. Valid token, wrong action label: request is rejected with a distinct reason.
3. Valid token from a hostname outside your allowlist: rejected.
4. Same token submitted twice: second call rejected as reuse.
5. Token held past its lifetime: rejected as expired, and the client re-runs the widget instead of showing a dead end.
6. Verification service unreachable or slow: the endpoint follows the fail-open or fail-closed choice you wrote down.
7. Retry of a request that failed after verification succeeded: returns the stored outcome through your idempotency key.
8. Missing token field entirely: rejected before any verification call is made.

Also test the human path on real devices, including a slow mobile connection and a browser with strict tracking protection, because script-loading failures look like "user failed the challenge" in your logs. Our guide to [bot false positive testing](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/bot-false-positive-testing-verify-visitors-before-blocking) walks through verifying real visitors before you turn on blocking.

## Measure completed legitimate actions, not challenge pass rates

A challenge pass rate is a vanity number. A high one can mean the challenge is easy for everyone, including automation. A low one can mean you are turning away customers. Neither tells you whether the signup, login or checkout is working.

Measure the outcome the business cares about: legitimate people who finished the action. For each protected endpoint, track a funnel with these counts per day:

- Page or form views that loaded the widget.
- Tokens issued, and tokens that reached your server.
- Verification results by reason: success, expired, reused, action mismatch, hostname mismatch, service error.
- Completed actions that later proved legitimate, such as verified emails, fulfilled orders, or accounts that were active after a week.

The last line is the one that matters, and you define it from your own records. A signup that never confirms its email isn't a completion. An order that is charged back isn't a legitimate one.

Compare these numbers before and after any change, whether that is swapping reCAPTCHA for Turnstile, adjusting a score cutoff, or adding a policy layer. If completed legitimate actions hold steady while junk submissions fall, the change helped. If both fall together, you blocked customers.

Segment by device class and by the verification failure reason, because an uptick in service errors from one region is an infrastructure problem, not a bot problem. And keep the raw reCAPTCHA scores or Turnstile outcomes in your logs for at least one full business cycle, so the next threshold decision rests on your history, not on a guess.

## Conclusion

Pick the widget your team can wire up correctly, then spend your effort on what surrounds it: exact action and hostname checks, one verification per token, an idempotency key for retries, and limits on the routes behind the login. A recaptcha vs cloudflare choice changes the response shape, not those four duties.


## Frequently asked questions

### What is the main server-side difference between reCAPTCHA and Cloudflare Turnstile?

Turnstile's Siteverify call returns a success boolean plus metadata such as hostname and action, so your code applies its own policy. reCAPTCHA v3 and Enterprise return a risk score that you must set a cutoff for from your own traffic. Verify current field names in each vendor's documentation before building.

### How long is a Turnstile or reCAPTCHA token valid, and can I reuse it?

Cloudflare's docs state a Turnstile token is valid for 300 seconds and can be validated once. Google's docs state reCAPTCHA response tokens expire after two minutes and are single-use. Treat any second verification of the same token as a replay, and confirm the current limits in each vendor's docs.

### Does a passed CAPTCHA protect requests after login?

No. A passed token covers only the request that carried it. Later calls ride on a session cookie, so protect sensitive routes with their own checks and account-level rate limits. Centinel Analytica applies allow, challenge or block policy through your existing CDN, so it can cover routes the widget never sees.

### Which fields should I validate besides the success flag?

Check the hostname against an allowlist of your own domains and require an exact match on the action label for each endpoint. Read both only from the vendor's verification response, never from the browser's request body. Log mismatches as their own rejection reason so probing is visible.

### How do I know whether my CAPTCHA is hurting real customers?

Track completed legitimate actions, such as confirmed signups or fulfilled orders, instead of challenge pass rates. Compare them before and after any change, and break verification failures down by reason and device.
