# WordPress Bot Protection: Login and XML-RPC Controls

Implement effective WordPress bot protection across login, XML-RPC, and REST endpoints behind your CDN without locking out editorial teams or syndication.

By Centinel Analytica. Published 2026-10-26.

Editorial teams live in their CMS, and when access breaks during breaking news, security teams hear about it immediately. Most WordPress hardening guides prescribe blunt solutions: password-protect everything at the edge, disable entire sub-systems, or install bloated plugins that run database queries on every incoming bot request.

For publishers running high-traffic WordPress clusters behind a CDN, blunt instruments fail. A blanket block on administrative paths blinds syndication partners, breaks mobile publishing apps, or locks out remote writers on dynamic residential IP addresses. It also shifts the CPU burden to PHP origins that already struggle under heavy catalog or article traffic.

WordPress bot protection is not a single switch. The platform has distinct administrative, legacy, and API surfaces. Each endpoint serves different actors, tolerates different authentication schemes, and needs its own edge controls.

## Inventory your WordPress endpoints before you restrict anything

Before writing a single WAF rule or touching edge configuration, trace your actual HTTP request flow. Too many infrastructure engineers treat WordPress as a black box and drop an immediate block on `/wp-login.php` or `/xmlrpc.php`. Then the syndication pipeline or an executive mobile app dies silently.

Map three exposed operational surfaces in your access logs. First is `/wp-login.php`, the human interactive entry point. Second is `/xmlrpc.php`, a legacy RPC endpoint that supports remote publishing, trackbacks, and certain Jetpack functions. Third is `/wp-json/`, the modern REST API that powers headless frontends, Gutenberg block editors, and third-party webhooks.

Pull 14 days of access logs from your CDN or origin web server. Group requests by path, HTTP method, client user agent, and status code. Look for POST requests to `/xmlrpc.php` returning HTTP 200, which point to active remote clients rather than simple port scans. Split `/wp-json/` requests into public unauthenticated GET reads and authenticated POST or PUT calls.

Map these footprints against your editorial calendar and you have a real baseline. A newsroom publishing 40 stories a day should not see 120,000 daily POST requests to `/wp-login.php`. Knowing that baseline separates operational traffic from brute-force sweeps before you enforce any thresholds. For larger media operations, cross-referencing this footprint with edge policies outlined in [bot mitigation for publishers](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/bot-mitigation-for-publishers-manage-unknown-crawlers-at-edge) prevents unintended downtime.

## wp-login.php: separate editors from credential-guessing traffic

Credential stuffing against WordPress login screens never stops, because automated tools scan the internet for unpatched sites daily. A single attack campaign can push origin CPU utilization above 90% just by forcing WordPress to calculate bcrypt password hashes over and over.

Your edge has to separate staff login attempts from bot-driven credential testing. Blocking `/wp-login.php` outright breaks editorial workflows, especially for distributed contributors who lack static corporate IP addresses. Moving the login URL to a custom slug like `/secret-login/` is security by obscurity. Scanners find it through redirection headers and standard discovery routines within minutes.

Enforce strict rate limits at your CDN edge on POST requests to `/wp-login.php`. Human writers do not submit passwords ten times a minute. Allow no more than 5 POST requests per five-minute window per client IP before triggering a challenge.

Require multi-factor authentication (MFA) within WordPress for all accounts with `edit_posts` capabilities or higher. If a bot guesses a valid password through distributed proxies, MFA stops the compromise at the second factor. Pair this with managed edge challenges for non-human behavioral signatures, so credential guessers get challenged at the edge before their requests ever reach PHP workers.

## XML-RPC: find legitimate dependencies, then disable, restrict or rate-limit

The XML-RPC interface (`xmlrpc.php`) is the largest systemic brute-force vulnerability in WordPress. Its batching methods allow automated tools to pack multiple authentication attempts into individual requests. A bot sending ten requests can execute 5,000 password guesses and slip right beneath traditional per-request rate limits.

First, find out whether your site needs it at all. In 2026, most modern WordPress architectures don't use XML-RPC. The WordPress REST API replaced almost all of its original functions. But legacy integrations, the native WordPress mobile app, Automattic's Jetpack plugin, and some third-party desktop editors still depend on it.

Inspect your CDN logs for legitimate traffic. If no approved external service or editor hits `xmlrpc.php`, return an immediate HTTP 403 Forbidden at the CDN edge. Don't pass these requests to origin Nginx or Apache web servers.

If your organization relies on Jetpack or an external syndication feed that requires XML-RPC, restrict access to verified upstream CIDR blocks. Automattic publishes its IP ranges, so edge-based IP whitelisting is straightforward. If you must leave it open for mobile app access across unknown networks, disable `system.multicall` through an Nginx rule or a targeted code snippet, and rate-limit POST requests hard.

## REST API: keep public reads open, protect authenticated writes

The WordPress REST API (`/wp-json/`) is an architectural problem because it serves two opposing needs. Public GET requests provide data for headless frontends, mobile viewports, feeds, and search features. Authenticated POST, PUT, and DELETE requests let editorial teams publish articles and manage site configuration.

Don't disable the REST API globally. Editorial interfaces rely on REST endpoints for everyday drafting and publishing tasks. Block the endpoint at the edge and post editing breaks across your entire newsroom.

Split your edge policies by HTTP method and route namespace instead. Public read requests to `/wp-json/wp/v2/posts` should hit your CDN cache with sensible cache-control headers, which takes the scraper load off your origin. Block public unauthenticated queries to `/wp-json/wp/v2/users`, which automated scrapers use to build username target lists for brute-force attacks.

For write operations, enforce authentication and challenge layers at the edge. Calls to `/wp-json/wp/v2/` with `POST`, `PUT`, or `DELETE` verbs should require explicit authorization headers or active session cookies. If a request claims to perform an editorial update without valid session state, drop or challenge it immediately.

## Client identity behind CDN and proxies: get rate limits keyed correctly

Rate limiting fails when your origin or edge keys against the wrong network attribute. When WordPress runs behind a CDN, forwarded requests may reach your origin carrying the CDN proxy IP as the network peer, while client details are passed in headers like X-Forwarded-For or CF-Connecting-IP. If your origin web server or a local WordPress security plugin keys its rate limits on `REMOTE_ADDR`, it will rate-limit the CDN edge node itself and take down the site for every visitor.

Configure your origin web server to read the true client IP from CDN-provided headers such as `CF-Connecting-IP`, `True-Client-IP`, or `X-Forwarded-For`. In Nginx, use the `ngx_http_realip_module` with an explicit list of trusted proxy CIDRs. Don't blindly trust headers from untrusted upstream connections, or attackers will spoof their client IP to bypass your thresholds. If you manage web tiers directly, configuring rules like those in [Nginx bot protection](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/nginx-bot-protection-rate-limits-real-ips-and-safe-rollout) ensures the right IPs get evaluated.

At the edge layer, IP-only rate limiting is no longer enough on its own. Attackers running automated credential attacks use commercial residential proxy networks to rotate through tens of thousands of IP addresses. A botnet may send one login attempt per IP per hour and sail past standard IP-based counters.

Key your edge rate limits on composite attributes: client IP, user-agent string, session cookie, and request path together. Where possible, deploy behavioral bot detection that profiles client execution instead of relying only on network address reputation.

## Nonces, Application Passwords and what they do not protect

WordPress ships with built-in security mechanisms that engineers sometimes mistake for bot protection. Knowing their limits prevents false assumptions about perimeter defense.

WordPress nonces do not protect against bot scraping or credential attacks. Despite the name, they are not true cryptographic nonces. They are hash tokens tied to a user session, an action, and a 12 to 24-hour time window. A bot making public requests or scraping public post content doesn't care about nonces. Even on authenticated forms, a scraper running a headless browser executes JavaScript, pulls the valid nonce from the page markup, and submits it with its payload.

Application Passwords, introduced in WordPress 5.6, let external scripts authenticate to the REST API without sharing primary user passwords. They isolate risk because administrators can revoke specific access keys without resetting an entire account.

But Application Passwords provide no rate limiting, no brute-force mitigation, and no proof of human interaction. An automated crawler that finds an Application Password through compromised CI/CD credentials or repository leaks can query the REST API unrestricted until origin limits halt it. Built-in WordPress security primitives defend against cross-site request forgery and credential reuse. They do nothing about automated high-volume traffic.

## Staged rollout: log, challenge, enforce, with rollback and false-positive tests

Never flip edge security rules straight to aggressive block mode on production WordPress. Even well-crafted regex patterns and rate limits produce false positives, and locking out a chief editor during breaking news causes organizational chaos.

Use a three-phase deployment pipeline:

First, run in log-only mode for at least seven days. Create edge rules that tag suspected bot traffic targeting `/wp-login.php` or REST endpoints and write those events to your SIEM or CDN logging bucket. Review the log stream against known internal traffic, syndication jobs, and remote staff access.

Second, move from logging to managed challenges. When traffic trips rate-limit thresholds or suspicious behavioral signatures, present a lightweight edge challenge instead of an outright HTTP 403. Real editors on residential proxies can pass browser verification, while headless scripts fail. During this phase, run systematic [bot false positive testing](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/bot-false-positive-testing-verify-visitors-before-blocking) across editorial teams before you proceed.

Third, shift to hard blocking only on verified threat patterns, such as multi-call XML-RPC requests or repeated challenge failures. Keep an explicit rollback toggle at the CDN level. If false-positive tickets spike, you need to step back to challenge mode within 30 seconds without rolling back application deployments.

Your CDN is good at caching static media, serving edge responses for cached HTML, and absorbing volumetric DDoS floods. Standard CDN caching rules offer little native defense against scrapers and bots that target dynamic endpoints like WordPress logins and API feeds.

Automated scrapers routinely bypass CDN caches by appending random query parameters, generating unique session identifiers, or hitting uncacheable POST routes directly. Standard WAF rules inspect request headers, but modern scraping tools easily spoof user agents and cycle residential IP addresses.

# HAProxy Bot Protection: Stick Tables and Rate Limits

Build practical HAProxy bot protection with stick tables, sliding windows, and maps. Learn where layer 7 rate limiting ends and edge challenges begin.

By Centinel Analytica. Published 2026-10-25.

When a wave of aggressive scrapers hits your origin, HAProxy is usually the first line of defense that doesn't fall over. Its event-driven core can track millions of connections without breaking a sweat, so it's tempting to push all bot mitigation logic straight into your load balancer config.

Community HAProxy has fast primitives for tracking abusive behavior. With stick tables, access control lists, and runtime maps, you can stop blunt denial-of-service attempts and aggressive content scraping in microseconds. But treating HAProxy like a full bot management engine is how production outages happen.

Effective haproxy bot protection requires understanding exact sliding window mechanics, key storage, and network boundaries. It also requires clarity on what simple rate counting can never catch. That clarity saves your engineering team from maintaining fragile config scripts every time attackers change tactics.

## What community HAProxy can and cannot do about bots (and how HAProxy Enterprise bot management differs)

Community HAProxy is an excellent traffic director and layer 7 policy engine. It is not a behavioral security platform. In the open-source edition, bot defense relies on deterministic traffic inspection: request paths, HTTP headers, request rates over time, TCP connection velocity, and IP reputations loaded into memory. You define strict thresholds, and HAProxy drops or tarpits traffic that violates them.

HAProxy Enterprise includes specialized security modules designed to classify automated clients. The commercial tier also bundles managed bot detection feeds and dedicated web application firewall layers that inspect payloads dynamically.

Community HAProxy focuses on request inspection rather than client-side browser challenges. It cannot execute JavaScript puzzles or inspect canvas rendering anomalies. If a scraper rotates residential proxy IPs and mimics regular user navigation cadences, open-source stick tables can't tell that scraper apart from a real customer.

What community HAProxy does well is high-throughput, rule-based policing. It drops misbehaving scrapers, caps burst traffic at the network edge, and defends authentication routes against volumetric brute-force attacks. Open-source HAProxy works on explicit request telemetry, not behavioral client profiling. Once you accept that, building stable policies gets much easier.

## Stick-table anatomy: type, size, expire and the stored counters

Every rate-limiting policy in HAProxy begins with the stick-table directive. A stick table is an in-memory key-value store built for concurrent, non-blocking lookups inside HAProxy worker processes. Misconfigure its parameters and you'll either exhaust system memory or evict active threat records too early.

A typical stick table definition requires four core parameters: name, key type, maximum size, and expiration time:

backend st_per_ip
  stick-table type ip size 1m expire 10m store http_req_rate(10s),http_err_rate(10s),conn_cur

The key type determines the indexing mechanism. `type ip` uses a 4-byte address key to store IPv4 addresses only, meaning it cannot represent IPv6 addresses. `type ipv6` uses a 16-byte address key and can store IPv6 addresses or IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses. For tracking tokens or session cookies, `type string` is available, though it requires setting a maximum key length.

The `size` parameter caps total stored records. `size 1m` reserves room for one million concurrent keys. If your site gets traffic from millions of distinct IP addresses, the table uses an LRU eviction strategy: older entries drop out to make room for new ones, which clears counters for slow-moving scrapers. Plan for roughly 64 to 128 bytes per entry depending on the counters stored. A table with one million entries takes roughly 100 megabytes of RAM.

The `expire` setting controls how long an idle key stays in memory after its last tracking update. Set it too short (say, 30 seconds) and a persistent scraper just pauses between bursts to clear its record. Set it too long and benign client IPs hog table capacity long after their sessions end. A window between 5 and 15 minutes is typical for rate tracking.

## track-sc0 and sc_http_req_rate: how the window actually behaves

To track a visitor, HAProxy ties incoming requests to a stick table slot using tracking counters, historically named `track-sc0`, `track-sc1`, and `track-sc2` (or modern numbered slots like `track-sc(0)`). Tracking has to happen before you evaluate rate limits, typically in an `http-request track-sc0` directive within your frontend or backend.

Many engineers assume `http_req_rate(10s)` calculates a rigid ten-second bucket that resets to zero every ten seconds. It doesn't. HAProxy uses an internal sliding window algorithm based on two adjacent periods. It tracks the count in the current period and blends it with the count from the preceding period, weighting the average by elapsed time.

This smoothing prevents the classic rate-limit hole where an attacker sends twice the allowed requests right at the border of a fixed window. It also means `sc_http_req_rate(0)` is an estimate, not an absolute integer tick count. If an IP sends 100 requests in one second and stops, its measured rate decays smoothly across the configured window instead of dropping off instantly.

frontend fe_main
  bind :443 ssl crt /etc/ssl/site.pem
  http-request track-sc0 src table st_per_ip
  http-request deny status 429 if { sc_http_req_rate(0) gt 50 }
  default_backend be_app

Tracking increments before evaluation happens. If a rule denies requests above 50, the 51st request increments the table counter and triggers the rejection rule immediately.

## Per-route thresholds with maps and the correct 429 deny

A single static rate limit across an entire application causes real usability problems. An interactive catalog with image carousels and API calls naturally produces higher burst rates than an account creation endpoint or a checkout submission. Hardcoding dozens of ACLs across multiple route paths makes HAProxy configs unmaintainable.

The clean pattern is pairing stick tables with HAProxy runtime map files. A map file stores key-value pairs that HAProxy searches using prefix, exact, or regex matching.

Create a map file at `/etc/haproxy/maps/rates.map` containing your sensitive paths and their corresponding limits:

/api/v1/auth/login 5
/checkout/pay 3
/catalog/search 40
/products 80

In your HAProxy config, look up the target path in the map. If the path matches, compare the client's current request rate against the retrieved numeric value. You can read more about coordinating endpoint rules across proxies in our guide on [Nginx bot protection](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/nginx-bot-protection-rate-limits-real-ips-and-safe-rollout).

frontend fe_web
  bind :443 ssl crt /etc/ssl/cert.pem
  http-request track-sc0 src table st_per_ip
  
  # Map lookup returns integer limit
  http-request set-var(req.rate_limit) path,map_beg(/etc/haproxy/maps/rates.map,0)
  
  # Check if route has an explicit limit and client exceeds it
  acl route_limited var(req.rate_limit) -m int gt 0
  acl rate_exceeded var(req.rate_limit),sub(sc_http_req_rate(0)) -m int lt 0
  
  http-request deny status 429 default-errorfiles if route_limited rate_exceeded

When rejecting bots, return HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) instead of a generic 403 or 500. Add a standard Retry-After response header when possible. A 429 tells well-behaved automated clients to back off and keeps your metrics clean in upstream log aggregators.

## Trusted client identity: PROXY protocol, X-Forwarded-For and shared-IP false positives

Tracking client IP addresses via `src` breaks the moment HAProxy sits behind an edge CDN, cloud load balancer, or reverse proxy. In that setup, `src` evaluates to the upstream CDN edge node, so HAProxy rate-limits the CDN and takes down your whole site.

To identify the true client IP, make sure your edge provider speaks PROXY protocol v2 to HAProxy. The PROXY protocol prepends connection metadata before the TLS or HTTP handshake, so HAProxy can set its internal `src` primitive directly to the client IP without inspecting HTTP headers.

If your architecture can't use PROXY protocol, extract the real IP from the `X-Forwarded-For` header. Never trust the raw header blindly, because any client can spoof arbitrary values. Tell HAProxy to accept `X-Forwarded-For` only from verified upstream proxy subnets:

acl from_trusted_cdn src 192.0.2.0/24 198.51.100.0/24
http-request set-var(req.client_ip) req.fhdr(x-forwarded-for,-1) if from_trusted_cdn
http-request track-sc0 var(req.client_ip) table st_client_ips if from_trusted_cdn

Even with accurate IP extraction, relying only on IP addresses causes false positives on shared network infrastructure. University campuses, corporate offices, mobile cell towers, and public Wi-Fi hotspots route hundreds of real users through single carrier-grade NAT (CGNAT) gateways. Low per-IP rate limits on catalog browsing will lock out genuine buyers.

Before dropping traffic outright, check whether the client claims to be a known search engine. Spurious web bots frequently forge user-agent strings. To avoid locking out real indexing bots while stopping impersonators, pair your stick-table limits with [fake Googlebot](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/fake-googlebot) verification.

## Inspecting tables and the reload and peers caveats

Debugging stick tables during an active incident means using the HAProxy Runtime API via the administrative UNIX domain socket. With `socat`, you can inspect active entries, dump rate metrics, and drop offending keys without restarting the process:

echo "show table st_per_ip" | sudo socat stdio /var/run/haproxy.sock
echo "show table st_per_ip data.http_req_rate gt 30" | sudo socat stdio /var/run/haproxy.sock
echo "clear table st_per_ip key 203.0.113.45" | sudo socat stdio /var/run/haproxy.sock

Stick tables carry a nasty hazard during service reloads. When HAProxy runs a hitless reload (`systemctl reload haproxy`), new worker processes spawn to handle new connections while old workers finish existing tasks. By default, stick-table state in community HAProxy lives in process memory and disappears when workers terminate.

To persist stick-table state across seamless reloads and share tracking counters across multiple HAProxy instances in an active-active cluster, configure a `peers` section:

peers local_cluster
  peer lb1 127.0.0.1:10240
  peer lb2 10.0.1.12:10240

backend st_per_ip
  stick-table type ipv6 size 1m expire 15m peers local_cluster store http_req_rate(10s)

Connecting HAProxy to local peer instances syncs table state over a dedicated TCP stream. When an old worker terminates after a reload, the incoming worker pulls historical counters directly from the peer process. Scrapers can't reset their rate penalty windows just because you pushed a config change.

## Where per-IP limits stop: low-rate distributed scraping and a rollout and test plan

Per-IP rate limits assume the attacker generates disproportionately high traffic volume from a concentrated pool of network addresses. Modern content scraping skips that assumption entirely.

Scraping frameworks rent pools of millions of residential proxy IPs. An attacker crawling an entire e-commerce catalog can rotate IP addresses on every single HTTP request. To your HAProxy stick tables, this looks like millions of distinct visitors making one request every five minutes. The counter for `http_req_rate(10s)` never exceeds 1, so table thresholds do nothing. If you're struggling with low-volume crawling, review our analysis on [price scraping protection](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/price-scraping-protection-test-controls-on-product-pages).

Scrapers also run headless Chromium or custom automation tools to mimic human navigation patterns. When basic IP throttling fails against distributed bots, you need behavioral classification and client-side proof-of-work challenges. That's where teams deploy dedicated edge protection like Centinel Analytica.

Centinel Analytica works alongside Cloudflare, CloudFront, Akamai, and Fastly, so your existing CDN and HAProxy stack stays intact while it identifies scrapers and AI crawlers that fly beneath per-IP thresholds. On a typical news site, 84% of requests claiming to be GPTBot were fake (Centinel Analytica, 2026). Dropping those unauthorized bots means verifying authenticity before they hit origin infrastructure.

Before enforcing aggressive HAProxy rules, run a phased rollout:
1. Audit your baseline traffic logs for peak per-route request velocities.
2. Deploy stick tables with `http-request track-sc0`, but use `http-request capture` or log flags to record would-be rejections instead of denying traffic.
3. Validate the rules against common false-positive vectors like corporate NATs and search engine crawlers.
4. Shift the action from logging to `http-request deny status 429` on sensitive endpoints first.

## Conclusion

HAProxy stick tables remain the right tool for baseline rate limiting, volumetric DDoS mitigation, and origin shielding. But when sophisticated scrapers spread their requests across massive proxy swarms, static IP limits hit a wall.

If distributed AI crawlers and automated scraping tools are draining your origin resources and bypassing your HAProxy rules, see how Centinel Analytica handles low-rate bots. # Imperva Advanced Bot Protection: Controls and Limits

Evaluate Imperva Advanced Bot Protection confidence levels, crawler policies, and API limits. Learn what vendor docs omit and how to verify bot traffic.

By Centinel Analytica. Published 2026-10-25.

Deploying bot protection inside an enterprise web application firewall often feels like signing a contract without reading the terms. You pick a policy, toggle a risk threshold, and trust the engine to tell paying customers from aggressive scrapers. Then headless browsers, residential proxies, and AI crawlers hit production routes, and the vendor documentation stops matching reality.

Imperva Advanced Bot Protection is one of the most visible enterprise products in this space. It promises automated bot detection across web, mobile, and API interfaces. But security engineers need to separate stated architecture from verified performance. Vendor capabilities are design goals, not guaranteed field results. Setting sane policies means knowing how Imperva classifies confidence, where client telemetry fails on API endpoints, and what evidence you have to gather yourself before switching policies to block.

## What Imperva Advanced Bot Protection, Imperva bot protection and Incapsula bot protection refer to

The naming around Imperva bot products confuses engineers who inherit legacy infrastructure. In June 2019, Imperva announced an agreement to acquire Distil Networks for its bot-management capabilities. Thales completed its acquisition of Imperva on December 4, 2023.

Legacy Incapsula bot protection means IP reputation lists, signature inspection, basic rate limits, and simple challenge pages built into the edge WAF. These controls catch high-volume scripts that send recognizable library headers like python-requests or cURL. They match known signatures against a static database of bad actors.

Imperva Advanced Bot Protection (often shortened to ABP) is described by the company as a multilayered detection engine. ABP runs either as a connector module with the Imperva Cloud WAF or as an inline plugin through web server agents and reverse proxies. Basic WAF rules can't do what ABP does: it injects JavaScript tokens into HTML responses to collect device fingerprints, inspect browser runtime APIs, assess mouse movements, and track request cadence across sessions.

When you evaluate Imperva bot protection, pin down which layer you're configuring. Basic WAF bot controls rely on static layer-7 request inspection. Advanced Bot Protection runs client-side code and analyzes behavioral intent. If you treat basic Incapsula rate limits as full bot defense, modern browser automation walks straight past your static rules.

## How Imperva describes bot confidence classification (High, Medium, Low, None) and what it implies for policy

Imperva Advanced Bot Protection sorts incoming traffic into four bot confidence tiers: High, Medium, Low, and None (Imperva, 2026). The vendor describes them as levels of certainty that a request comes from an automated tool and not a human visitor.

High confidence means the engine found clear signs of automation. That includes direct runtime signals like active WebDriver flags, CDP automation hooks, known scraping signatures, or fingerprint mismatches where reported headers contradict hardware capabilities. Medium confidence means suspicious behavior with incomplete telemetry, such as requests from hosting providers or known residential proxy pools with no clear client-side browser execution. Low confidence covers slight statistical deviations from baseline user paths. None means the traffic looks like normal human interaction.

The tiers read simply on paper, but they carry big operational trade-offs. A classification is an internal probability model mapped to a bucket, not absolute truth. High confidence usually gives you enough justification to block or drop traffic. Medium confidence is where production environments break down.

Set Medium to block, and you will block real users on corporate proxies, VPNs, low-end mobile devices, or privacy-focused browsers that restrict client-side JavaScript. Set Medium to allow, and sophisticated scrapers with randomized pauses and rotating residential IPs pass through untouched. Treat confidence ratings as proof instead of signals, and you get revenue-hurting false positives or unchecked scraping.

## Policy decisions: matching action to confidence, intended visitors and the cost of false positives

Every bot policy rule maps an enforcement action to a confidence level. Imperva describes response options that vary across confidence tiers, including allow, block, challenge, rate-limit, and monitor. Picking the right one means putting a price on errors for each endpoint.

On e-commerce checkout flows or enterprise login endpoints, a false positive costs revenue and customer goodwill immediately. Blocking a genuine buyer at payment because their browser failed a canvas fingerprint check hurts business metrics directly. On these critical paths, High confidence traffic warrants a silent block or simulated error. Medium confidence traffic needs a gentler verification route. That means running [bot false positive testing](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/bot-false-positive-testing-verify-visitors-before-blocking) to audit session telemetry before you enforce hard drops.

JavaScript challenges and CAPTCHAs are common defaults, and they add real friction. A browser challenge can take several seconds to execute, which breaks single-page application flows and mobile web views. When legitimate visitors see challenge screens often, drop-off rates climb. Commercial scraping operators also bypass simple visual CAPTCHAs with cheap automated solver farms, so a challenge often annoys humans while failing to stop determined bots.

For catalog pages, content feeds, and publisher articles, the math flips. A false negative lets competitors or content scrapers extract entire databases, which raises backend load and infrastructure costs. On these routes you can afford a stricter stance on Medium confidence traffic, as long as you watch origin metrics for sudden drops in organic human traffic. Never apply one global enforcement action across your whole web property.

## AI assistants and crawlers: visibility versus control, and what to verify about licensing and scope

Imperva documentation stresses visibility into commercial bots, search engines, and AI tools through predefined categories in its management console. The platform documents the identification of AI crawlers and agents, including OpenAI's GPTBot and Anthropic's ClaudeBot.

Visibility is not control. A dashboard badge confirming that an AI crawler hit your site protects nothing if your edge policy lets unauthenticated requests through. And if you trust user-agent declarations without verification, your origin is wide open to impersonators. Many scraping operators deliberately spoof legitimate crawler strings to evade rate limits.

Centinel Analytica research showed that on a typical news site, 84% of requests claiming to be GPTBot were fake. Attackers claim to be well-known search engines or AI assistants because they know legacy rulesets often whitelist those agents. You need to check whether your security controls verify reverse DNS lookups or published ASN IP ranges, as covered in our analysis of [fake Googlebot](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/fake-googlebot) detection methods.

Publishers also need to verify licensing scope and robots.txt behavior. Major AI labs claim to respect robots.txt exclusion rules, but secondary scraping aggregators and stealth AI models ignore robots.txt directives entirely. If you want to stop unauthorized content ingestion, advisory standards won't do it. You need active edge policies that demand verifiable proof of crawler identity and hard-drop unauthorized scrapers.

## Browser traffic versus API and mobile traffic: where evidence and challenges differ

Bot detection works very differently depending on the protocol and client environment. For browser traffic, Imperva ABP injects a client-side JavaScript snippet that inspects the browser. The script checks screen dimensions, installed fonts, WebGL capabilities, audio contexts, and DOM implementation quirks. These checks make standard browser scraping noisy and detectable.

API endpoints and native mobile apps break that model. A mobile app talking over REST or GraphQL doesn't run a desktop web engine. It doesn't parse injected JavaScript tokens or run canvas rendering tests. Apply browser-oriented bot policies to pure API endpoints, and they fail because the expected client-side telemetry never arrives.

Protecting APIs and mobile backends means inspecting different evidence layers: TLS fingerprinting (JA3 or JA4 signatures), HTTP/2 frame parameters, client token attestation, and behavioral request sequencing. Scrapers know this gap. When attackers go after pricing data, product inventory, or user accounts, they often drop desktop web scrapers and point their scripts at the mobile API instead.

When teams test scraping services with [residential proxy scraper detection](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/residential-proxy-scraper-detection-how-to-test-scraping-services), they routinely find that mobile endpoints leak data even when desktop pages trigger challenges. Bot defense on APIs can't depend on DOM inspection. It has to analyze edge telemetry and request cadence at the network boundary.

## Evaluation limits: what vendor documentation cannot tell you and the evidence to collect yourself

Vendor documentation gives you architectural blueprints and feature summaries. It can't tell you how the detection algorithms perform against offensive tools aimed at your own assets. Sales decks highlight high capture rates but skip the evasion vectors modern headless browsers actually use.

To evaluate any bot defense solution objectively, collect direct evidence across three vectors:

1. Real-browser stealth bypass: Modern scrapers use automation frameworks like Camoufox, Browserbase, or custom CDP-based drivers that spoof hardware profiles and slip past standard JavaScript fingerprint checks. Centinel Analytica published benchmark research testing eight scraping tools against seven vendors. Real-browser automation bypasses generic behavioral thresholds when fingerprinting checks are shallow.

2. Edge telemetry audit: Vendor dashboards show aggregated, sanitized charts. Export raw HTTP access logs and compare the ratio of challenged requests against confirmed user sessions. Look for sessions where a visitor finished a multi-step checkout or account registration despite a suspicious risk score from the edge engine.

3. Integration latency: Measure the millisecond overhead from client-side token generation, challenge validation, and origin proxy routing. Adding 200 milliseconds to time-to-first-byte on international routes directly damages core web vitals.

## Fallback and rollback: monitor-first rollout, exception handling and a link to the full proof-of-concept scorecard

Deploying bot protection straight into blocking mode is an outage waiting to happen. A reliable rollout is phased and keeps application availability and safe rollback paths first.

Start with a monitor-first deployment lasting at least 14 days. Configure every detection rule to log without challenging or dropping connections. Pipe the logs into your SIEM or analytics cluster. Cross-reference flagged IP addresses and session IDs against legitimate business events, support tickets, and conversion goals. If legitimate enterprise partners or corporate mobile users trigger Medium or High confidence alerts, fix your exception rules before you turn on enforcement.

Build hard exception paths into your edge layer. Define secure bypass headers, HMAC-signed tokens, or IP allowlists for critical third-party integrations, monitoring probes, and trusted payment gateways. Give your operations team an automated, single-command rollback that switches enforcement to passive pass-through if an engine update flags genuine customer cohorts.

## Conclusion

Vendor documentation describes how an engine is supposed to classify bot traffic. Only live traffic analysis shows how the detection tiers behave against modern scraping stacks. Treat confidence categories as absolute guarantees and you will either lose revenue to false positives or expose proprietary data to headless browser automation. Demand verifiable telemetry, test your defenses with offensive automation, and roll out in monitor mode first.

# Azure Bot Protection: Front Door WAF Rules and Safe Deployment

Deploy azure bot protection safely across Front Door and App Gateway. Learn Bot Manager 1.1 rule overrides, JS challenge limits, and safe detection rollout.

By Centinel Analytica. Published 2026-10-23.

A security team deploys an Azure Web Application Firewall policy, turns on the managed bot ruleset, and expects commercial scrapers to disappear overnight. Two weeks later, headless browsers are still pulling catalog pricing while real search engine crawlers trigger automated blocks because an internal partner IP failed a reverse DNS verification rule.

Native azure bot protection is not an autonomous fraud prevention system. It is a collection of Layer 7 inspection filters, IP reputation lists, and rule groups split across Microsoft edge and regional services. Platform and security engineers have to configure these rules on purpose. To make native Azure WAF controls work, you need to know where edge routing ends and regional routing begins, what Bot Manager 1.1 actually inspects, and how to roll everything out safely.

## What 'Azure bot protection' means here: WAF controls, not Bot Framework

Microsoft uses the word bot across unrelated product families. Azure Bot Service and the Bot Framework provide developer SDKs and cloud runtimes for building conversational chatbots. Those services handle dialogue trees, customer service chat endpoints, and speech processing. They have nothing to do with stopping malicious traffic at your perimeter.

In network and security operations, Azure bot protection refers specifically to bot-management rules that identify good, bad, and unknown bots, rather than serving as a general term for perimeter controls built into Azure Web Application Firewall. These controls operate at HTTP Layer 7. They inspect incoming request headers, check client IP addresses against threat intelligence feeds, run rate limits, and apply custom rule logic before traffic reaches application compute.

These WAF mechanisms are stateless inspection pipelines. When an HTTP request reaches an Azure perimeter service, the WAF engine runs it through the configured rule sets. The engine then issues one of several discrete actions: Allow, Log, Block, Redirect, or Challenge. It does not track application-level account history or build post-authentication behavioral graphs. It checks whether incoming HTTP requests look like legitimate browser traffic or automated scripts, based on predefined signatures and network telemetry.

## Front Door vs Application Gateway: global edge and regional WAF are different services

Azure offers two ingress services that host its WAF engine: Azure Front Door and Azure Application Gateway v2. Mixing up their placement leads to wasted architecture and inflated origin bandwidth bills.

Azure Front Door is a global edge routing and content delivery service. When you attach an Azure WAF policy to Front Door, rule evaluation happens at the edge point of presence nearest to the client. Malicious traffic and crude scraper bursts get dropped at the network edge, before they cross Microsoft backbone networks to your origin region.

Application Gateway v2 is a regional Application Delivery Controller running inside your own Azure Virtual Network. Its WAF evaluates requests only after traffic enters your specific Azure region. If you rely only on Application Gateway for bot mitigation, automated scrapers eat regional gateway throughput and public IP bandwidth before the WAF drops a single packet.

The two rule engines also get features on different schedules. Front Door receives Microsoft threat intelligence feed updates and managed bot rule versions ahead of regional Application Gateway. Application Gateway v2 supports the Core Rule Set (CRS) and a basic Bot Manager ruleset, but it has no edge-level caching or global distribution. If your application uses Front Door at the edge, put your primary bot controls on that Front Door WAF policy. Use Application Gateway WAF for internal routing controls or compliance boundaries behind the edge.

## Standard custom rules vs Premium managed bot rules

Azure Front Door splits bot controls between two pricing tiers: Standard and Premium. The split decides whether you write manual signatures or consume Microsoft managed threat intelligence.

Front Door Standard supports custom WAF rules only. On Standard, bot defense means building match conditions yourself. You can match on client IP address, geographic location, request method, request URI, query strings, and request headers like User-Agent. You can also enforce basic rate limiting per client IP over one-minute or five-minute sliding windows. Standard has no managed bot threat feeds. If a residential proxy network rotates IP addresses while scraping your site with a desktop Chrome User-Agent, a Standard WAF rule can't identify the client as automated.

Front Door Premium adds managed rule sets. These include the Default Rule Set (DRS 2.0 and DRS 2.1) and the Microsoft Bot Manager Rule Set (Microsoft_BotManagerRuleSet). Premium policies ingest daily data feeds gathered by Microsoft Threat Intelligence, covering known scrapers, commercial crawler services, search engine ranges, and malicious scanning infrastructure.

Custom rules on Standard work well for predictable problems, like rate-limiting an internal login route or blocking unapproved geographic jurisdictions. They fail against modern scraping pipelines. Teams running edge platforms like Cloudflare, Fastly, or CloudFront alongside Azure can pair the edge with specialized detection like [Centinel Analytica](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/).

## Bot Manager 1.1: BadBots, GoodBots and UnknownBots, default actions and overrides

The primary managed ruleset in Azure Front Door Premium is Bot Manager 1.1. Microsoft divides it into three rule groups: BadBots, GoodBots, and UnknownBots.

The BadBots group targets known malicious automation. That covers commercial content scrapers, vulnerability scanners, and automated exploitation tools. In Bot Manager 1.1, rules under BadBots default to the Block action. When an inbound request matches an IP or fingerprint tied to scanning tooling, Front Door returns an HTTP 403 Forbidden.

The GoodBots group is designed to accommodate legitimate search engines and partner crawlers. The default action for GoodBots is Allow. Microsoft verifies these bots with reverse DNS validation and internal IP reputation tables. If a request sends a Googlebot User-Agent header but fails reverse DNS validation, the engine does not treat it as a GoodBot. It reclassifies the request under BadBots or UnknownBots. You need to understand this mechanism when diagnosing [fake Googlebot](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/fake-googlebot) patterns in raw server access logs.

The UnknownBots group targets automated clients that can't be verified as benign or malicious. That includes generic headless utilities, Python requests libraries, and unverified commercial bots. Bot Manager 1.1 sets UnknownBots to the Log action by default.

Leaving defaults untouched is a common operational error. If an enterprise site needs to allow an unverified third-party indexing service or a specific partner crawler, the security lead must create an explicit rule override. In the Azure portal or your Infrastructure as Code definitions, you can expand the ruleset, select a specific Rule ID, and change the action from Block to Allow, or disable the rule entirely. Manage overrides per endpoint path. Otherwise you open broad security holes across your whole domain.

## JavaScript challenge: where it fits and what the documentation says it does not cover

Azure Front Door Premium includes an active client challenge mechanism: the JavaScript challenge action. Instead of returning an immediate HTTP 403 block or 200 pass, the WAF returns an intermediary HTML response containing an encrypted JavaScript challenge payload.

The client browser executes the JavaScript, completes a proof-of-work computation, and writes an authentication cookie back to the client context. The browser then resubmits the original HTTP request with the cookie attached. Front Door validates the cookie and routes the traffic to the origin. This flow filters out simple cURL scripts, basic Python requests, and dumb scrapers that don't evaluate client scripts.

Microsoft documentation spells out the operational boundaries of this challenge action. First, it breaks pure API clients. If your endpoint serves iOS or Android native apps, microservice API calls, or webhooks, a JavaScript challenge breaks those clients. Native mobile HTTP libraries don't parse HTML or run JavaScript runtimes, so the WAF drops those calls as failed challenges.

Second, JavaScript challenges don't stop modern headless browser scrapers. Tools built on Puppeteer, Playwright, or anti-detect browser forks run full Chromium, WebKit, or Firefox rendering engines. They execute the challenge script, generate the verification cookie, and keep scraping. When scrapers pair these headless engines with [residential proxy scraper detection](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/residential-proxy-scraper-detection-how-to-test-scraping-services) avoidance techniques, standard edge JavaScript puzzles can't prove whether the client is a human or a script.

## Safe deployment: Detection vs Prevention, rule priority, log queries, narrow exceptions and rollback

Enabling WAF rules straight in Prevention mode invites site outages. A safe deployment follows a five-step operational lifecycle: Detection mode, priority mapping, log validation, narrow exceptions, and instant rollback.

Always deploy a new Azure WAF policy in Detection mode. In Detection mode, Front Door evaluates rules, assigns matches, and logs events to your Azure Log Analytics workspace without altering HTTP traffic. Let the policy run for at least seven business days to capture weekday and weekend traffic patterns.

Get rule evaluation priority right. Custom rules execute first, ordered numerically from lowest priority number to highest. If a custom rule matches a request with an Allow action, later custom rules and managed rules are skipped. Managed rule sets, including Bot Manager 1.1 and DRS, execute after custom rules. To exempt an external automated partner from Bot Manager, create a custom rule with a priority lower than your general rate limits.

Inspect your deployment using Kusto Query Language (KQL) in Azure Log Analytics. Query the `FrontDoorWebApplicationFirewallLog` table to see what the engine would have blocked:

```kusto
FrontDoorWebApplicationFirewallLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where action_s == "Block" or action_s == "Log"
| summarize Count = count() by ruleName_s, clientIP_s, userAgent_s, requestUri_s
| order by Count desc
```

Look through this data for legitimate internal tools, enterprise customers with corporate proxy pools, and marketing automation systems. When Bot Manager catches legitimate traffic, build narrow exceptions. Don't disable an entire rule group. Add a custom rule matching the specific request path combined with an authenticated partner token or client IP subnet. Thorough [bot false positive testing](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/bot-false-positive-testing-verify-visitors-before-blocking) during this validation phase prevents production interruptions.

Define an automated rollback plan before switching to Prevention mode. Your deployment pipeline needs a single command, via Azure CLI or Terraform, that reverts the WAF policy to Detection mode in under two minutes if conversion metrics drop.

## Test plan and evaluation: user journeys, accessibility tools, approved crawlers, cache and origin impact, and where native rules stop

Before finalizing your WAF configuration, run an evaluation across five validation categories.

First, validate critical user journeys. Test user login, password recovery, product catalog pagination, and checkout sequences. Script these flows with your test automation framework while simulating realistic user header configurations. Make sure your internal synthetic monitoring nodes (such as Datadog or New Relic Synthetics) use dedicated User-Agent strings and whitelisted IPs, so your own monitoring doesn't trigger bot rules.

Second, test accessibility tools and assistive clients. Screen readers and automated accessibility testing suites often emit non-standard HTTP header combinations. Confirm that accessibility testing tools can crawl and render the site without getting WAF challenge pages.

Third, verify approved search crawlers. Check Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools daily during rollout and watch the crawl error graphs. A sudden spike in 403 or 503 errors means your bot configuration is intercepting valid search indexers, because of strict reverse DNS matching or misconfigured custom rules.

Fourth, monitor cache and origin impact. Front Door caches content at the edge. If your bot rules apply challenge cookies or redirect headers, verify that the edge doesn't cache challenge responses and serve them to later visitors. Verify that legitimate bot blocks lower origin CPU and database utilization as expected.

Fifth, know where native rules stop. Azure Front Door Premium Bot Manager is an effective outer gate against volumetric scrapers, simple automation, and known threat infrastructure. It cannot verify advanced browser automation. Published research shows that on a typical news site, 84% of requests claiming to be GPTBot were fake (Centinel Analytica, 2026). When scrapers use residential proxies and headless automation engines, native WAF rules lack the behavioral telemetry to tell human interaction from machine automation.

## Conclusion

Native Azure bot protection is a necessary perimeter baseline for any workload routed through Front Door or Application Gateway. It strips out noisy vulnerability scanners, known malicious IPs, and crude scraping scripts before they eat regional compute. But static threat intelligence and rudimentary JavaScript puzzles are not comprehensive automation security. Treat them that way and your origin stays exposed to residential proxy networks and headless browser automation.

Centinel Analytica covers the gaps that native edge WAF rules leave behind. It identifies scrapers and AI crawlers. It works alongside your existing CDN and edge infrastructure, so your CDN or WAF stays in place. Protect your endpoints with [Centinel Analytica](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/) to address the headless automation currently slipping past your WAF rules.


## Frequently asked questions

### Can Azure Front Door WAF stop scrapers using residential proxies?

Azure Front Door managed bot rules struggle against scrapers operating on residential proxy networks. Because residential proxies rotate through millions of legitimate consumer ISP IP addresses, static reputation feeds rarely flag them. If the scraper runs a headless browser that passes basic JavaScript challenges, native WAF rules see the traffic as legitimate. Specialized detection from Centinel Analytica integrates with your edge to tell real visitors from scrapers.

### What is the difference between Bot Manager 1.0 and 1.1 in Azure Front Door?

Bot Manager 1.1 refines Microsoft bot categorization and default actions. It introduces explicit separation between GoodBots, BadBots, and UnknownBots. BadBots default to Block, GoodBots default to Allow with reverse DNS validation, and UnknownBots default to Log. Version 1.1 reduces false positives compared to 1.0 by offering better granularity for rule-by-rule overrides and tighter integration with Microsoft Threat Intelligence feeds.

### Will enabling JavaScript challenges break mobile apps or REST APIs?

Yes. The JavaScript challenge action requires the client to execute a client-side JavaScript script and return an encrypted cookie. Native iOS and Android mobile apps, backend API integrations, and command-line clients like cURL do not execute JavaScript. If you apply JavaScript challenges to paths serving non-browser clients, those requests will fail. You must exclude pure API routes using custom WAF rules.

### How do I verify if Googlebot is being blocked by Azure bot protection rules?

Check your Azure Log Analytics workspace using KQL to query the FrontDoorWebApplicationFirewallLog table. Filter for requests where the User-Agent contains Googlebot and the action is Block. If you see blocks, check the ruleName_s field. Legitimate Googlebot traffic is blocked if it fails Microsoft reverse DNS checks or if an aggressive custom rate limit rule takes priority over Bot Manager rules.

# Akamai Bot Protection: Policies, Bot Scores, and Tests

Configure Akamai bot protection with confidence. Learn how bot scores work, tune policy thresholds by endpoint, and test defenses against modern scrapers.

By Centinel Analytica. Published 2026-10-23.

An operations team opens Akamai Control Center on a Monday morning after a spike in origin load. The traffic graph shows a clean, uniform elevation across catalog pages, but the origin CPU hit 92 percent. Thousands of requests carry bot scores in the 60 to 80 range, yet none triggered an automated block.

Akamai Bot Manager is one of the most widely deployed bot defense solutions in enterprise networks. It processes client telemetry, compares behavioral markers, and gives every request a score between 0 and 100. That one number often decides whether a user passes through, gets a challenge, or is dropped at the edge.

Treating that score as an absolute verdict creates blind spots. A single static threshold will either block real users or let distributed scrapers drain origin resources. Managing akamai bot protection well means understanding how those scores are calculated, setting policies that match endpoint sensitivity, and checking decisions with rigorous evaluation tests.

## How Akamai Bot Manager scores requests: 0 human to 100 bot, and what that does and does not tell you

Akamai Bot Manager assigns an integer score from 0 to 100 to incoming HTTP requests. A score near 0 means strong human characteristics. A score near 100 means high confidence of automation. Between those extremes sits a gray zone where client telemetry is incomplete, ambiguous, or deliberately obscured.

To produce the score, Akamai evaluates several telemetry vectors at once. In browsers, client-side JavaScript sensors collect input dynamics, device orientation, touch events, and browser environment properties. At the protocol layer, it analyzes HTTP/2 frame settings, TLS cipher suites, and TCP window sizes. Behavioral heuristics track request rates, navigation timing, and odd path traversal across sessions.

The score tells you how closely a client matches known automation profiles or verified human profiles. It doesn't tell you business intent. A score of 78 means edge heuristics saw abnormal execution timing or missing browser attributes. It doesn't mean the visitor is a hostile scraper. A corporate employee behind a secure enterprise web proxy, or an automated procurement script run by a commercial partner, can easily land in that same bracket.

Sophisticated scrapers running Playwright or Puppeteer with stealth patches spoof these telemetry signals on purpose. When a scraping operation routes traffic through residential proxies, the network signature looks identical to legitimate consumer broadband. If you rely on an edge score without understanding the signal distribution behind it, you either leak proprietary data or raise your false positive rate.

## Cautious, Strict and Aggressive response segments: configurable boundaries, not universal thresholds

Akamai builds its policy engine around response profiles, typically Cautious, Strict, and Aggressive. These profiles group score bands into three operational zones: definitely human, suspicious, and definitely automated. Akamai provides recommended default boundaries, but these segments are configurable markers, not universal laws.

In a Cautious configuration, the edge rarely takes disruptive action. Requests might only face an outright block above a score of 90, with soft challenges between 75 and 89. This profile suits public content portals where every dropped reader hurts ad revenue or SEO reach. The trade-off is heavy scraper leakage. Automation frameworks that keep their scores in the 60s will walk straight past the defenses.

An Aggressive configuration flips the balance. It might challenge traffic starting at a score of 40 and issue 403 Forbidden responses at 65. E-commerce sites during flash sales and ticketing operations often shift to this posture to stop automated inventory hoarding. The danger is collateral damage. Real customers on older mobile devices or low-bandwidth connections often fail to return complete sensor payloads in time, which pushes their scores into the challenge zone.

Threshold selection is not a one-time deployment decision. Teams need to analyze their score distributions under normal traffic before picking boundaries. Running [bot false positive testing](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/bot-false-positive-testing-verify-visitors-before-blocking) shows security teams how many actual customers fall into the target challenge segment. Thresholds have to reflect what an error costs on that specific host.

## Approved crawlers and the known bot directory: allowing Googlebot and others without trusting a user agent string

Every web property needs legitimate search engines and social preview bots to index its pages. Blocking Googlebot hurts organic visibility within hours. Opening a broad exception based on the User-Agent header invites trivial evasion. Scrapers have spoofed search engine identifiers for decades.

Akamai handles this with its Directory of Known Bots. Instead of trusting client-supplied strings, the platform verifies identities through automated cryptographic and network validation. If a request claims to be Googlebot but comes from a consumer hosting provider or an unverified autonomous system, Akamai flags it as a spoofed bot and applies an immediate mitigation action.

Newer AI web crawlers make this directory harder to manage. AI operators deploy automated crawlers to train models or answer real-time search queries. Security leads must decide whether to treat these crawlers as legitimate search partners or aggressive harvesters. In published research, Centinel Analytica found that on a typical news site, 84 percent of requests claiming to be GPTBot were fake. Attackers pose as AI bots on purpose to get around perimeter controls.

Commercial crawlers now need different treatment from search indexers. Teams must configure policies that separate verified search indexers from aggressive AI data collectors, and terminate impersonators outright. You can read more about spotting these spoofing patterns in our technical breakdown of [fake Googlebot](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/fake-googlebot) behavior.

## Endpoint-specific policy: login, search, product and pricing pages, APIs, and data exports

A single uniform bot policy across your whole host will break critical workflows. Different endpoints carry very different risk profiles, payload characteristics, and performance tolerances. Akamai policies need to be segmented by URI path, HTTP method, and client type.

Authentication endpoints need your strictest enforcement. Credential stuffing and account takeover attacks hit `/login` and `/auth/reset`, so these routes should use aggressive score boundaries. If client telemetry is missing or anomalous on a login POST request, challenge or drop the traffic immediately. Legitimate users expect strict security during sign-in, and the business cost of credential stuffing far outweighs the minor friction of an interactive challenge.

Catalog search, product detail, and pricing endpoints call for a different strategy. Retailers and publishers can't afford to interrupt potential buyers with interactive challenges. Meanwhile, automated price scrapers constantly target these routes to undercut margins. Teams dealing with competitors harvesting inventory data should implement targeted defenses, as detailed in our guide to [price scraping protection](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/price-scraping-protection-test-controls-on-product-pages). On these endpoints, silent mitigations such as tarpitting, serving cached alternate views, or feeding altered price datasets often work better than hard blocks, which tell the bot developer to change their script.

APIs and data export routes need separate handling. Native mobile apps calling API endpoints do not execute standard browser JavaScript sensors. If your mobile APIs share host paths with web APIs without proper SDK tagging, aggressive bot score rules will accidentally cut off your mobile user base.

## Evidence to gather before changing a threshold or action: monitor first, segment logs, and check legitimate workflows

Switching a bot response action from alert to block without log evidence is the fastest way to cause a production incident. Before tightening any boundary in Akamai Control Center, security teams need a baseline of raw telemetry.

Keep new configurations in monitor mode for at least two business cycles, which usually means two weeks. Use Akamai DataStream 2 or Cloud Monitor to stream log events into your SIEM. Every log entry should include the assigned bot score, the bot score reason code, the verified bot classification, the URI path, and client network identifiers like ASN and country code.

Segment this log data to isolate edge cases. Check the score distribution for corporate egress IPs. Enterprise users often exit through shared gateways or cloud-hosted virtual desktops that alter network timing and produce elevated bot scores. If your company sells B2B software, an aggressive threshold on registration pages will block your highest-value prospects.

Review partner integrations and webhook endpoints too. Many business partners consume public pricing or availability feeds through automated scripts that don't run JavaScript telemetry. If those partner requests lack dedicated API keys or mutual TLS certificates, an automated policy will classify them as high-scoring bots. Document every approved automated workflow before you convert monitor actions into active mitigations.

## Evaluation tests for Akamai bot protection, and where a layer like Centinel fits alongside it

A bot management policy is only as dependable as the tests that validate it. Vendor dashboards give a false sense of security as a measure of your defensive strength. If an automated script evades detection, the dashboard just marks that traffic as human. To the dashboard, the attack never happened.

Engineering teams should run realistic adversary simulations against their own endpoints. Don't test with basic Python Requests or cURL commands, because Akamai catches those elementary tools without difficulty. Run tests with actual headless browser stacks instead: Playwright with stealth configurations, Puppeteer with canvas and WebGL mocking, and modified browser forks. Route these test sessions through residential proxy providers to see whether your Akamai rules can detect behavioral scraping when the IP reputation looks completely clean.

A benchmark tested eight scraping tools against seven vendors and found large performance gaps once tools emulate human browser quirks. This is where an additional inspection layer fits.

Centinel Analytica provides bot and AI crawler protection that tells real visitors from scrapers and applies allow, challenge or block policy through your existing CDN or edge. It approaches the problem from the perspective of modern scraper architecture. Deployed next to Akamai, it helps security teams pinpoint the advanced headless automation and distributed scraping networks that slip through standard edge score bands.

## Next steps: run a traffic audit or book a demo

Bot traffic needs continuous refinement. As commercial scraping operations adopt new browser automation frameworks, static edge scores lose effectiveness over time.

Start by auditing your current Akamai Bot Manager policy deployment. Check which endpoints run on global default profiles and convert them to route-specific configurations. Audit your known bot exception lists to confirm that IP validation is strictly enforced on all search and AI crawlers. Make sure monitor mode logs feed your security analytics pipeline, so threshold changes are backed by concrete telemetry data.

If automated scrapers, price harvesters, or unauthorized AI crawlers keep getting through, consider adding specialized detection logic to your edge stack. Contact Centinel Analytica to run a traffic audit or book a demo, and see how reverse-engineered detection protects your data without disrupting your infrastructure.

## Conclusion

Trusting vendor-provided bot scores blindly guarantees operational friction. Scrapers change their browser evasion tactics weekly, while real users browse from increasingly fragmented device environments. Configure your Akamai bot protection rules at the route level, verify every automated crawler with cryptographic network checks, and test your defenses with realistic browser tests. Akamai Bot Manager assigns a score from 0 to 100 based on client-side telemetry, network fingerprints, and behavioral analysis. Rather than applying a single global threshold, teams should segment policies by endpoint risk, such as login routes, search pages, and pricing APIs.
