# AWS Bot Protection: WAF Bot Control Levels and Safe Deployment

Deploy native AWS bot protection using WAF Bot Control. Learn the difference between Common and Targeted inspection, rule labels, and safe Count mode rollouts.

By Centinel Analytica. Published 2026-10-23.

Engineering teams running production traffic through CloudFront or Application Load Balancers eventually find the same thing in their access logs. Scrapers eat origin capacity, pollute analytics pipelines, and inflate cloud bills. The fastest reaction is to open the AWS console and turn on native bot protection inside the existing web access control list.

AWS WAF Bot Control gives you a direct way to inspect automated traffic, but switching it on without understanding how it works starts fires. Default blocking actions will take down legitimate partner feeds, break native mobile app requests, and block the automation your own teams rely on every day. Native bot mitigation in AWS is not a toggle. It's a signal engine that needs deliberate configuration, targeted scope-down rules, and a disciplined rollout.

## What AWS bot protection means: WAF Bot Control in the web ACL

Native AWS bot protection runs mostly through the AWS WAF Bot Control managed rule group, identified in configuration templates as AWSManagedRulesBotControlRuleSet. This managed rule set attaches directly to a web access control list (web ACL) associated with Amazon CloudFront distributions, Application Load Balancers (ALB), Amazon API Gateway endpoints, or AWS AppSync GraphQL APIs.

You don't need custom regular expressions or manual IP blacklists. The rule group inspects incoming HTTP request headers, TLS connection attributes, and client IP reputation pools maintained by AWS threat research teams. When an edge location or load balancer receives a request, the web ACL evaluates rules in strict numerical priority order. If Bot Control sits at priority 10, it sees the request before any rule at priority 20 can.

One architectural detail matters most. Bot Control doesn't just emit an allow or block verdict. Its main job is to inject namespaced metadata labels into the request context inside the web ACL. These labels describe the identity, category, and behavior of the client. A monitoring tool, a verified search engine crawler, and an unauthorized scraper all get tagged with structured signals. How your web ACL responds to those signals depends entirely on the downstream rules you write.

## Common vs Targeted: what each inspection level detects

AWS splits Bot Control into two tiers: Common inspection and Targeted inspection. Pick the wrong one and you either leave your origin exposed to scrapers or add client-side overhead you didn't need.

Common inspection is a passive layer. It analyzes the HTTP request stream and requires no client-side script execution. It identifies known, widespread automation: search engine crawlers from Google and Bing, SEO assessment tools, uptime checkers, and basic automation libraries such as cURL, Python Requests, Go-http-client, and Scrapy. It verifies legitimate crawlers using reverse DNS lookups and IP validation tables. If an unauthorized script claims to be Googlebot from a commercial cloud IP address, Common inspection tags it as an impersonator. Because it works only on request headers and network metadata, it adds zero latency for end-user browsers.

Targeted inspection moves from passive inspection to active interrogation of the client. It goes after sophisticated, motivated scrapers: headless browser automation built on Puppeteer or Playwright, stealth scraping frameworks, credential stuffing tools, and bots running through residential proxy networks. The client must acquire and submit an encrypted authorization token. Targeted inspection then verifies browser environment integrity, execution timing, and client interaction telemetry. The choice between the two is a choice between lightweight signature filtering and active behavioral challenges.

## Labels are signals: custom rules, label matching and rule-action overrides

The most common mistake teams make with AWS Bot Control is leaving the managed rule group on its default blocking actions. Default actions vary across individual rules—CategoryHttpLibrary blocks only unverified bots, while SignalAutomatedBrowser defaults to Block—and these actions can interrupt legitimate traffic if left unadjusted. In production, that breaks business integrations. Enterprise customers query your APIs with Python scripts, internal batch jobs fetch data with cURL, and monitoring providers trip automated browser heuristics.

Treat Bot Control as a signal generator, not an executioner. The right deployment overrides the entire rule group, or individual member rules, to Count mode. In Count mode, the rule group runs its full inspection pipeline and appends labels to the request context without terminating the connection.

AWS WAF labels follow a hierarchical namespace, such as awswaf:managed:aws:bot-control:bot:category:http_library or awswaf:managed:aws:bot-control:signal:automated_browser. Once these labels exist in the request context, you write custom WAF rules below the Bot Control managed rule set to take deliberate action.

A custom rule can check for a bot label and for specific operational exceptions at the same time. For example, you can block requests carrying the label awswaf:managed:aws:bot-control:signal:known_bot_data_center only when they hit /checkout or /login, while letting the same requests reach your public documentation paths. You can also let specific IP CIDR blocks or custom authorization headers bypass enforcement even when Bot Control marks them as automation.

## Targeted prerequisites: tokens, the AWS WAF JavaScript SDK and rule group version (check current docs before you pin)

Moving from Common to Targeted inspection brings technical prerequisites that change your application architecture. Targeted Bot Control relies on silent challenges and encrypted tokens stored in cookies or custom headers.

For traditional server-rendered websites, CloudFront can inject challenge scripts into HTML responses automatically. For single-page applications built on React or Next.js, and for native iOS and Android apps, automated HTML injection fails. You have to integrate the AWS WAF JavaScript SDK into your client build pipeline or use the mobile SDK wrappers. The client app must initialize the SDK, run the telemetry challenge in the background, and include the resulting token in the headers of later API calls. If your mobile team ships API changes without initializing the SDK, legitimate mobile users get blocked at the edge.

Rule group versioning takes strict operational discipline. AWS updates managed rule definitions continuously to track new scraper signatures. In Terraform, CloudFormation, or the AWS CDK, you can track the default version or pin a specific version string. Pinning protects you from unexpected signature changes on a Friday afternoon. But pinned versions age fast, and AWS deprecates older rule group versions on published schedules. You need a maintenance routine to test and bump versions quarterly. Check current AWS documentation for version lifecycles before you hardcode a version string in your infrastructure repository.

## Scope-down statements and cost drivers (without quoting prices)

Running AWS Bot Control across every inbound HTTP request to your CloudFront distribution or Application Load Balancer wastes budget. AWS charges a monthly managed rule group fee alongside request charges that incorporate tier-specific allowances and usage rates depending on whether you run Common or Targeted inspection. Targeted inspection carries a much higher variable multiplier than Common inspection.

If your web ACL sits in front of a content publisher or an ecommerce storefront, most incoming requests are static assets: cached images, CSS stylesheets, client-side JavaScript chunks, and web fonts. Scrapers don't steal catalog data by downloading your favicon ten thousand times. They go after dynamic HTML routes and JSON API endpoints. Inspecting static asset requests with Bot Control burns budget and doesn't improve your security.

Use scope-down statements on the Bot Control rule group to limit what gets inspected. A scope-down statement defines the criteria a request must meet before AWS WAF runs the managed rule group. Set yours to inspect requests only when the URI path starts with sensitive prefixes such as /api/, /products/, /catalog/, or /news/. Or invert the logic and skip inspection when the URI path matches static file extensions (.png, .css, .js, .woff2) or when the request carries a cache-hit header from your CDN edge. Restrict evaluation to dynamic application paths and your variable inspection volume covers only the requests where bot defense matters.

## Safe rollout: Count mode, log review and a test checklist

Rolling out AWS Bot Control safely takes a staged deployment over several weeks. Jump straight to blocking mode and you will have an incident.

Start by deploying the Bot Control managed rule group with every individual rule action overridden to Count. Enable AWS WAF full request logging. Configure the web ACL to stream logs to an Amazon S3 bucket, an Amazon CloudWatch Logs log group, or an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream. Make sure log filtering doesn't drop the labels array, because that array holds the diagnostic data you need.

Use Amazon Athena or CloudWatch Logs Insights to analyze captured traffic. Run queries that aggregate by client IP, User-Agent header, URI path, and matching Bot Control labels. Find false positives before you enforce blocking rules. Look for customer automation, internal health checks, search engine spiders, and marketing vendor webhooks that triggered unexpected bot signals.

Run this pre-enforcement checklist across your staging and production environments:

1. Verify verified crawler routing: Confirm that legitimate search engine traffic from Google, Bing, and major indexing platforms receives the awswaf:managed:aws:bot-control:bot:verified label and bypasses rate limits.

2. Test programmatic integrations: Run automated integration tests, mobile app test suites, and third-party webhook payloads against the web ACL to confirm none of them are flagged as hostile scraping frameworks.

3. Verify scope-down statements: Check your WAF logs to confirm that static media and asset paths don't log Bot Control evaluation events.

4. Configure CloudWatch metrics and alarms: Build CloudWatch dashboards that watch the CountedRequests and BlockedRequests metrics emitted by the Bot Control namespace. Set an alarm to alert your on-call engineers if the volume of counted bot signals surges unexpectedly.

5. Phased rule activation: Once your log review comes back clean, don't switch the whole rule group to Block at once. Move individual custom rules to CAPTCHA or Challenge first, watch client completion rates for seven days, and only then enable terminal Block actions for confirmed malicious labels.

## Limits of native Bot Control and where an add-on alongside CloudFront fits

Native AWS Bot Control gives you a baseline defense inside the AWS ecosystem, but dedicated scraping operations get around standard WAF defenses easily. Modern scrapers don't run crude cURL scripts from commercial data center IPs. They use anti-detect browser binaries with forged canvas fingerprints and route requests through distributed residential proxy networks.

When a scraping operation spreads requests across millions of residential IP addresses, IP reputation heuristics stop working. Many malicious crawlers also spoof real browser identities or impersonate well-known search crawlers. [Centinel Analytica](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/) found that on a typical news site, 84% of requests claiming to be GPTBot were fake. Basic WAF checks that evaluate static header combinations struggle to catch these impersonators without false positives for real human visitors.

When native WAF rules hit their limit, publishers and ecommerce teams add specialized edge intelligence. Centinel Analytica works alongside CloudFront, Cloudflare, Akamai, and Fastly. It leaves your existing CDN and WAF architecture in place and separates real visitors from scrapers. Security teams can then enforce allow, challenge, or block policies at their existing edge without rebuilding their AWS infrastructure. To test your current detection against evasive tools, read our analysis of [residential proxy scraper detection](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/residential-proxy-scraper-detection-how-to-test-scraping-services) and our guide on [bot mitigation for publishers](https://www.centinelanalytica.com/blog/bot-mitigation-for-publishers-manage-unknown-crawlers-at-edge).

## Conclusion

Native AWS Bot Control gives you an immediate way to tag and manage basic automated traffic directly inside your web ACL. But relying only on native managed rules leaves your application open to modern scraping tools that rotate residential proxies and spoof legitimate crawler identities.

If you run high-value content or pricing catalogs on CloudFront, ALB, or API Gateway, check whether your current WAF rules actually catch modern headless scrapers. A small Berlin team of former bot builders and reverse engineers built Centinel Analytica to provide bot and AI crawler protection that works alongside CloudFront, so you can apply challenge, allow, or block policies at your existing edge. Request a traffic audit with Centinel Analytica to see what slips past your native AWS WAF rules.


## Frequently asked questions

### What is the difference between AWS WAF Bot Control Common and Targeted inspection?

Common inspection uses static request-data analysis, evaluating attributes such as user-agent strings, IP addresses, and other request characteristics without requiring an SDK. Targeted inspection adds detection for bots that do not self-identify, using techniques like browser interrogation, TLS fingerprinting, behavioral heuristics, and machine learning to defend against credential stuffing and advanced scraping.

All use cases

  • Scraping and AI crawlers→

    Scrapers and AI crawlers copy your prices, product catalogue, and articles page by page, often through a real browser on residential IP addresses. Competitors undercut you with your own prices, and AI services answer with your content without sending the reader to your site.

  • Account takeover→

    Credential-stuffing bots try leaked username and password pairs against your login form at machine speed, often from a new IP address on each attempt. Every match is a working account the attacker drains, resells, or uses for the next fraud.

  • API abuse→

    Bots call your API directly, so none of the checks that run in the browser apply. They pull data in bulk, test stolen credentials, or book stock faster than a person can. Each call can look like a request from your own app, and you pay for the server load and any paid service behind it.

Common questions

What site owners ask before deployment.

How is this different from our CDN or WAF?

Your CDN and WAF stay in place. Centinel adds crawler verification and browser-side evidence for automation that looks like ordinary visitor traffic. Check what your current setup already detects on the routes that matter. Then test whether Centinel's evidence changes a decision on the traffic your setup misses.

What did the September 2026 benchmark test?

We ran eight scraping and browser-automation tools against seven products: Centinel, Akamai, Cloudflare, DataDome, Fastly, HUMAN Security and Kasada. The tools were Browser-use, Firecrawl, Browserbase, kernel.sh, Playwright Stealth, Camoufox, Zyte and Ulixee Hero. We recorded whether each product detected each tool. The results are our observations from the configurations we tested. Plans and settings differ, so test your own routes and traffic before you choose.

Why does Centinel check the browser?

Headers can be copied, so they do not show whether a person or a script sent the request. Where the integration supports browser collection, Centinel adds runtime and session evidence from the browser. Judge that evidence against the workflow it protects and your access policy.

Will visitors see a CAPTCHA?

Centinel's browser checks run automatically. The response a visitor receives depends on the integration and your policy. During your evaluation, test challenge behaviour, accessibility and session continuity.

Can we allow trusted crawlers while blocking scrapers?

Yes. Centinel separates declared and verified crawlers from spoofed or hidden automation, so your team can apply a different access policy to each traffic class.
